options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds (max 600000 for a foreground command)

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to modify

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: ListAgents
tools.description: Lists agents you can SendMessage to — in-process subagents you spawned, the teammates on your team, other local Claude sessions on this machine, your Claude sessions running in the cloud (when this session has cloud access; a cloud session receives your message but cannot message any session back yet — do not ask it to reply, read its answer in its own transcript), and (when Remote Control is connected here) your account's other sessions — Remote Control sessions on other machines and cloud sessions, each row labeled by kind. Names are the address: send with `SendMessage({to: "<name>", message: "..."})`, copying the name exactly as a row prints it. Append a row's ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — two rows share it, or an error asks you to disambiguate.

channel.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

q.description: Not available in this build; leave unset.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read

offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once

limit.description: The number of lines to read. Only provide if the file is too large to read at once.

pages.description: Page range for PDF files (e.g., "1-5", "3", "10-20"). Only applicable to PDF files. Maximum 20 pages per request.

allow_large.description: Set to true to read a text file, or a line range of one, that is over the usual size limits, up to what still fits in your context. Only use this when you genuinely need all of it or the user asked for the whole file; otherwise read it in parts with offset and limit, or search it.

tools.name: ReportFindings
tools.description: Report code-review findings as a typed list so the host UI can render them. Use this only when the active code-review instructions tell you to report findings with this tool; otherwise follow whatever output format those instructions specify. When reporting a review's results, call it once with the verified findings ranked most-severe first (empty array if nothing survived verification) and do not also print the findings as text. When re-reporting after applying fixes (only if the apply instructions ask for it), set `outcome` on each finding to what actually happened.

findings.description: Verified findings, most-severe first; empty if none survived

file.description: Repo-relative path of the file the finding is in

short_summary.description: Compressed label for compact UI (≤60 chars): the claim alone, no rationale or consequence clause

category.description: Short kebab-case slug of the finding type, e.g. "correctness", "simplification", "efficiency", "test-coverage"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

content.text: Tool loaded.

  **Version:** the text is arXiv 2505.19828v1, "SecVulEval: Benchmarking LLMs for Real-World C/C++ Vulnerability Detection", marked "Preprint. Under review". PDF p. 1 shows the same five York University authors, so it is the right paper; only the title changed. Analyst notes say the analysis is based on the preprint and Table 3 should be re-checked against the published AIware 2026 version.
  
  **Summary:** A de-duplicated C/C++ benchmark: 25,440 functions, 5,867 CVEs, 145 CWEs, with statement-level labels and context labels generated by GPT-4.1. Five LLMs run in a 5-agent pipeline on 300 manually judged functions. The best, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, reaches 23.83% statement-level F1 and 53.89% function-level F1. There are no SAST, deep-learning or single-prompt baselines.
  
  **Evidence rows:**
  - RQ1 [V] p. 8, moderate: statement-level F1 is 23.83% (Claude), 22.38% (GPT-4.1), 15.31% (Codestral), 13.57% (Qwen), 7.14% (Deepseek). Function-level F1 is 35.20–53.89% and function-level precision is at most 47.41%.
  - RQ2 [V] p. 8, moderate: requiring the correct statements plus correct reasoning more than halves F1 (GPT-4.1: 52.25% → 22.38%).
  - RQ2 [V] p. 3, p. 6, moderate: the dataset has 0% duplicates; earlier datasets have up to 18.9%.
  - RQ2 [I] p. 7, p. 8, p. 13, moderate: the statement-level recall seems to be computed differently from the paper's own definition (see below).
  - RQ4 [V] p. 13, moderate: detected functions have a median of 14–33 lines of code, missed ones 64–71 (Mann-Whitney p ≤ 0.0168 for all five models).
  - RQ4 [A] p. 13, weak: GPT-4.1 and Claude over-flag CWE-476, CWE-416 and CWE-190. They flagged 214–215 of 300 functions as vulnerable when 120 were.
  - RQ5 [V] p. 9, moderate: models identify the needed context poorly (at most 41.33% per context type; function arguments at most 5.31%; environment context 0%).
  - RQ3 [V] p. 17, moderate: open 22–33B models take about 5–8 minutes per function on 4 × L40S GPUs.
  
  **Surprising or doubtful:**
  - **Recall inflation.** I rebuilt whole-number counts from Table 3 and the flag counts on p. 13 (Claude: 215 flagged, 90 correct at function level, 119 vulnerable, 33 correct at statement level). Every reported statement-level recall comes out exactly as statement-level hits ÷ (statement-level hits + functions missed entirely). So "right function, wrong reasoning" cases were not counted as misses, although p. 7 says they should be. Under the paper's own definition, Claude's recall would be about 27.7% (not 53.23%) and F1 about 19.8% (not 23.83%). GPT-4.1's recall would be about 26.1% (not 49.21%). This is my inference, labelled [I].
  - The implied number of vulnerable functions differs by model (119–126), although the paper says 120.
  - The context "ground truth" was generated by GPT-4.1, which is also one of the models evaluated on it.
  - 300 samples, a single run, and no confidence intervals.
  
  **Incomplete sections:** none.
  
  ## shu2026evaluating · ready · full-text
  **Version:** the text is arXiv 2506.07503v2 (10 Mar 2026, 53 pages), recorded in the file.
  
  **Summary:** Eight pre-trained code models or embedding encoders (CodeBERT, CodeT5/CodeT5P, UniXcoder, LineVul, 3 OpenAI embedding encoders) are compared with five LLMs (zero-shot, few-shot with 3 retrieved examples, instruction tuning) on REEF across seven languages, at function and line level. On balanced data, fine-tuned GPT-4o with retrieved few-shot examples (GPT-4o ITFSP) beats CodeT5P (accuracy 0.7196 vs 0.6037; line-level F1 0.6641 vs 0.4841). On the imbalanced set (~17% vulnerable) the pre-trained models win. There are no SAST or graph-network baselines.
  
  **Per-language numbers:**
  - Function-level accuracy, GPT-4o ITFSP / CodeT5P: C 0.7557/0.5081, C# 0.7273/0.6136, C++ 0.7901/0.5249, Go 0.8082/0.6062, JavaScript 0.6642/0.7062, Java 0.7169/0.6031, Python 0.6626/0.5623 (p. 21).
  - Line-level F1, GPT-4o ITFSP / CodeT5P: C 0.5478/0.3727, C# 0.4348/0.4750, C++ 0.5774/0.4768, Go 0.7078/0.4146, JavaScript 0.7815/0.6556, Java 0.6391/0.4167, Python 0.6055/0.4519 (p. 26).
  
  **Evidence rows:**
  - RQ1 [V] p. 17, moderate: on balanced data GPT-4o ITFSP beats CodeT5P (accuracy 0.7196 vs 0.6037; MCC 0.4360 vs 0.2860), but F1 is tied (0.7069 vs 0.7075).
  - RQ1 [V] p. 17, p. 37, moderate: prompt-only LLMs, including GPT-4o, GRACE, DeepSeek-R1 and QwQ-plus, are near chance (accuracy 0.36–0.53, MCC ≤ 0.07).
  - RQ1 [V] p. 23, p. 26, moderate: line-level F1 is 0.6641 vs 0.4841, but CodeT5P has the higher AUC (0.8644 vs 0.8116).
  - RQ2 [V] p. 40–41, moderate: on the imbalanced set the ranking flips. UniXcoder gets F1 0.4626 and CodeT5P MCC 0.3627, vs GPT-4o ITFSP at 0.4010 and 0.2774.
  - RQ2 [V] p. 39, moderate: on 2024–2025 CVEs, function-level accuracy is 0.7874 but line-level F1 drops from 0.6641 to 0.3450.
  - RQ2 [I], weak: possible split leakage and inflated line-level metrics (see below).
  - RQ3 [V] p. 42, moderate: GPT-4o tuning costs $86.07 vs about $5.59 per local A6000 training run (~15x cheaper).
  - RQ4 [V] p. 21, p. 26, moderate/weak: best function-level language is Go and worst is Python; line-level F1 is best in JavaScript (0.7815) and worst in C# (0.4348, only 13 test functions).
  - RQ4 [V] p. 30, weak: memory-safety CWEs are hardest to localise (CWE-787 6.25%, CWE-119 21.74%, CWE-125 27.27%).
  - RQ4 [V] p. 34, weak: functions only the LLM gets right are more complex and longer than those only the pre-trained model gets right; the pre-trained model does better on deeper nesting.
  
  **Surprising or doubtful:**
  - The paper says GPT-4o ITFSP beats all models "across all seven languages" (function level, p. 22). Its own p. 21 numbers contradict this for JavaScript: CodeT5P 0.7062 and CodeT5 0.6898 vs GPT-4o 0.6642.
  - The result rests on one configuration. GPT-4o ITFSP is the only LLM setting clearly above chance (the next best is 0.5874), and few-shot makes every other model worse. There are no seeds or tests, though "significantly" is used throughout.
  - **Possible leakage [I]:** the split is random at function level, each vulnerable function's fixed twin is in the data labelled clean, and few-shot examples are retrieved from the training set. Only exact-match filtering is applied, so a near-identical twin can sit on the other side of the split.
  - **Line-level metrics [I]:** the always-vulnerable baseline has precision 0.0267, but the dataset has about 14.3% vulnerable lines. That fits metrics computed over 113 padded line slots per function, which would inflate accuracy and false-positive rate.
  - Accuracy on the 2024–2025 split (0.7874) is higher than on the original test set (0.7196), which is unexplained.
  - Several numbers in the text differ from the tables (CodeBERT accuracy, GPT-3.5 zero-shot, UniXcoder MCC, imbalanced GPT-4o F1), and the model is called "GPT-4" in places. Training details and how GPT-4o was fine-tuned are not reported.
  
  **Incomplete sections:** none. Several figures are bar charts that did not extract as text, so per-language values for models other than GPT-4o and CodeT5P are not available.

The 4 analyses on deep learning and data quality are done, so 9 of 20 are complete.

**Main finding:** older vulnerability datasets have very unreliable labels; only 24–60% of the "vulnerable" labels are correct. Some test sets also contain up to 19% exact copies of their training data. On a realistic dataset, deep learning models' F1 drops from about 68% to about 2–21%.

**First contradiction found:**
- A 2023 study says fine-tuned models are far ahead of ChatGPT, at 94% vs 29% F1.
- A 2025 study (PrimeVul, a cleaned-up dataset) finds GPT-4 ahead of fine-tuned models on a test that checks whether a model can tell a vulnerable function from its fixed version.
- My working explanation, which is our own interpretation, is that the benchmarks differ: the 2023 dataset's data leakage favours fine-tuned models. This is central evidence for RQ2.

The other 2 analysis agents are still running: the head-to-head studies and the project-scale/agent studies.

content.content:
## SUMMARY PER KEY

**li2026llm** · ready · full-text (arXiv 2601.19239v2, 25 Sep 2026)
- Compares 5 specialized LLM detectors (RepoAudit, KNighter, IRIS, LLMDFA, INFERROI) and 2 general coding agents (Codex/GPT-5.4, Claude Code/Sonnet 4.6) with CodeQL, Semgrep, SpotBugs and Clang Static Analyzer (CSA). Test sets: 265 known C/C++ and Java vulnerabilities (8 CWEs) and 24 real-world projects.
- The general agents have the highest recall (59.55% C/C++, 64–82% Java). Specialized tools and SAST often have near-zero recall and a 75–100% sampled false discovery rate (SFDR, the share of sampled warnings that are false). Cost reaches $1,247.66 and 225M input tokens per project.
- Surprising or doubtful:
  - Codex is both an evaluated tool and the TP/FP labeller. It also gets the lowest SFDR (9.09%), and that figure rests on only about 22 warnings.
  - "Precision" on the controlled set only counts false positives inside known vulnerable files.
  - The appendices (A–C) are not in the PDF.

**guo2025repoaudit** · ready · full-text (arXiv 2501.18160v3, 29 May 2025; its p. 1 already carries the ICML 2025 / PMLR 267 footer)
- An LLM agent that audits whole repositories (Claude 3.5 Sonnet). On 15 projects it finds 40 true positives (TP) against 11 false positives (FP), 78.43% precision, at $2.54 and 0.44 h per project. Meta Infer finds 7 TP / 2 FP; Amazon CodeGuru finds 0 TP / 18 FP.
- In nine further projects it reports 185 new bugs, 174 of them confirmed or fixed.
- Surprising or doubtful:
  - It conflicts with li2026llm on overlapping Linux and ImageMagick targets. li2026llm finds RepoAudit recall of 0–5.71% and SFDR of 92.77–95.41%.
  - Recall here only means reproducing 21 known bugs.
  - The paper doesn't say how RepoAudit's own TP/FP labels were decided.
  - Internal inconsistencies: "ten" vs "nine" repositories; the MLK column of Table 4 adds up to 75, not the printed 76.

**yildiz2025benchmarking** · ready · full-text (ACL 2025)
- Introduces JITVul: 879 CVEs from PrimeVul, 91 CWEs, 1,758 paired vulnerable/fixed functions in C/C++. It compares a plain LLM, a dependency-augmented LLM and a ReAct agent (GPT-4o / 4o-mini), each with CoT and few-shot prompting variants.
- F1 stays around 48–66% while pairwise accuracy (pAcc, both versions of a pair labelled correctly) stays at or below 20.17%. ReAct gives the best pAcc.
- Surprising or doubtful:
  - There is no SAST, deep-learning or cost comparison.
  - Every GPT-4o/4o-mini pAcc is below the 25% that random guessing would give.
  - In the appendix, DeepSeek-Coder-V2 with dependency augmentation reaches F1 82.09 / pAcc 69.24, which contradicts the "ReAct is better" conclusion for that model.
  - Several pAcc values are exact multiples of 1/119, which suggests some settings ran on about 119 pairs, not 879. This is my inference; the paper doesn't say.

**tan2026think** · ready · abstract-only (no OA full text)
- A study on PrimeVul Pair with three phases: instruct vs thinking (reasoning) model variants, single/dual/multi-agent designs, and explanation quality.
- Thinking modes raise F1 in 7 of 8 settings, mainly through recall, and use 2.7–4.4× more energy. The dual-agent design has the best F1 but flags 88.2% of functions as vulnerable.
- Sections 3–6, 8 and 10 say "full text not available". Its evidence should carry less weight. The user would need to supply the ASE 2026 PDF for a full analysis.

  ## zhou2024comparison · ready · full-text (arXiv v1, preprint, not peer-reviewed)
  **Summary:** Compares 15 free SAST tools with 12 open LLMs of 8B parameters or less (fine-tuned, LoRA, zero-shot, CoT, few-shot) on whole repositories in Java, C and Python (270 CVEs). It reports no precision or F1, only detection ratios and the share of functions flagged. SAST detects up to 44.4% of CVEs while flagging 0.2–5.2% of functions; LLMs detect up to 100% but flag 3.5–77.4% of functions.
  
  **Evidence rows:**
  - RQ1: best SAST is 37.5% (Horusec, Java), 44.4% (CodeQL, C), 30.0% (DevSkim, Python); many tools detect 0%. (p. 6–7, V, weak)
  - RQ1: LLMs reach 90–100% detection but flag 3.5–77.4% of functions. (p. 6–7, V, weak)
  - RQ1: LoRA fine-tuning beats prompting: Java 73.4% detection with 19.4% flagged. (p. 7, V, weak)
  - RQ1: GPT-3.5 detects only 3.7–23.2%. (p. 10, V, weak)
  - RQ2: vulnerable functions are 0.008–0.18% of all functions; flagged-function share is used as a stand-in for the false-positive rate. (p. 3, 5, V, moderate)
  - RQ2: test sets are about 8–10 CVEs per language. (p. 6, I, weak)
  - RQ3: running all SAST tools together raises detection by 25–100% relative to the best single tool. (p. 8, V, weak)
  - RQ3: voting across LLMs cuts the flagged share by 40.9–74.6%. (p. 9, V, weak)
  - RQ3: no SAST+LLM hybrid is tested. (I, moderate)
  - RQ4: CWE-119 and CWE-476 are detected best; CWE-835 and CWE-89 are missed by both families. (p. 8, V, weak)
  - RQ4: combined LLMs work best for Java, combined SAST for C and Python. (p. 9, A)
  - RQ5: authors recommend filtering, repository context and repo-level evaluation. (p. 10, A)
  
  **Problems found:**
  - Table 3 contradicts the text and figures. It shows Horusec at 7.5 (text 37.5), CodeQL C at 4.4/3.3 (text 44.4/33.3) and DevSkim at 0.0/0.0 (text 30/20). I checked the rendered PDF and the cells are truncated there too.
  - The abstract and conclusion say that ensembling SAST tools with LLMs reduces the drawbacks of both, but no such ensemble was run.
  - Test sets are tiny, inferred from detection ratios that move in 12.5, 11.1 and 10-point steps.
  - The split is random by CVE with no grouping by project, so the same project can appear in training and test.
  - The "ESEC/FSE'23" page header is a template artefact, not a sign of publication.
  
  ## gnieciak2025large · ready · full-text (arXiv v1; published in IEEE Access 2025)
  **Summary:** Compares SonarQube, CodeQL and Snyk Code (default settings) with zero-shot GPT-4.1, Mistral Large and DeepSeek V3 on 10 small C# projects with 63 vulnerabilities. Mean F1 is 0.797/0.753/0.750 for the LLMs vs 0.260/0.386/0.546 for the SAST tools; LLMs always give the wrong line or column and invent "outdated dependency" findings.
  
  **Evidence rows:**
  - RQ1: mean F1 as above. (p. 10, V, weak)
  - RQ1: mean recall is 0.78–0.88 for LLMs vs 0.19–0.52 for SAST; mean precision is 0.72–0.78 vs 0.57–0.69. (p. 10, V, weak)
  - RQ1: pooling the raw counts (my arithmetic) gives SAST precision 0.81–0.87 vs LLM 0.74–0.79, and Snyk F1 about 0.70. (p. 8, I, weak)
  - RQ2: LLMs get credit for findings at the wrong location; each tool ran once; projects were written by the authors. (p. 5–6, 8, V, moderate)
  - RQ3: runtime per project is about 186–213 s for CodeQL, 14–29 s for Snyk and 3.5–67 s for the LLMs. (p. 9, V, weak)
  - RQ3: authors recommend LLMs for early triage and SAST for audits, but test no hybrid. (A)
  - RQ4: covers only C# SQLi, XSS, secrets, command injection, weak crypto and outdated dependencies, with no per-category results. (V, weak)
  - RQ5: open problems are localisation and hallucinated findings. (p. 11–12, A)
  
  **Problems found:**
  - The abstract calls the projects "real-world", but the methods say they were "prepared" with "a random number of vulnerabilities" and are 3–5k characters each, which points to seeded test code.
  - LLMs are credited for findings at the wrong line or column; SAST tools get no such allowance.
  - When a tool reports nothing on a project, its precision is set to 0 and still averaged in, which drags SAST precision down.
  - Pooled counts change the false-positive picture: GPT-4.1 has the most false positives (19), not DeepSeek. Snyk's share of false reports (15/57) is about the same as the LLMs'.
  - The abstract mentions developer effort and a thematic analysis; neither is reported.
  - Temperature, model versions and run cost are not reported. The paper refers to itself as "this thesis".
  
  ## khare2025understanding · ready · full-text (arXiv v3; published at ICST 2025)
  **Summary:** Tests 16 LLMs with 3 prompts on 5,000 balanced single-function samples (OWASP, Juliet Java and C/C++, CVEFixes Java and C/C++; 25 CWEs). Compares them with CodeQL on the synthetic sets only, and with DeepDFA and LineVul on CVEFixes C/C++.   **Evidence rows:**
  - RQ1: best LLM averages 62.8% accuracy; real-world accuracy is 10.5% lower than synthetic. (p. 5, V, moderate)
  - RQ1: CodeQL vs best LLM, accuracy/F1: OWASP 0.63/0.72 vs 0.60/0.65; Juliet Java 0.94/0.94 vs 0.76/0.79; Juliet C/C++ 0.72/0.61 vs 0.65/0.72. (p. 9, V, moderate)

  - RQ2: many configurations answer "vulnerable" every time (precision 0.50, recall 1.00, F1 0.67), which is the trivial result on a 50/50 set. (p. 16, I, moderate)
  - RQ2: CodeQL is run on synthetic data only, and the best LLM is picked after seeing results from 48 configurations. (V, moderate)
  - RQ3: a dataflow-style prompt raises real-world F1 by up to 0.18; sources and sinks are correct in 16–18 of 20 checked samples. (p. 5–6, V, weak)
  - RQ3: authors propose LLMs finding sources/sinks for a static analyser to reason over. (A)
  - RQ4: LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-22, 78, 476 and 416 (up to +24%); CodeQL is better on CWE-190 (+11–21%). (p. 8, V, moderate)
  - RQ4: LLMs do well on self-contained CWEs and poorly on context-dependent ones (CWE-862, C/C++ out-of-bounds). (p. 7, V, moderate)
  - RQ5: missing global context is the main failure cause. (p. 7, A)
  
  **Problems found:**
  - The headline F1 of 0.71 is barely above the always-"vulnerable" result of 0.67.
  - The abstract says LLMs beat CodeQL; that holds only for certain CWEs, not overall.
  - Table V lists DSCoder-15B with a size of "33B".
  - The appendix wording on CVEFixes labels reads as reversed.
  - No cost data, and no code or data link in this version.
  
  ## dubniczky2025castle · ready · full-text (arXiv v2; published as an LNCS chapter, venue_kind "book"; metadata has no abstract)
  **Summary:** Introduces CASTLE, 250 hand-written single-file C programs (mean 42 lines, 25 CWEs, 150 vulnerable and 100 clean). Evaluates 13 static analysers, 2 formal verification tools and 10 LLMs using a new author-defined CASTLE Score. GPT-o3-mini scores 977, o1 962, R1 956 and GPT-4o 954, vs ESBMC 661 and CodeQL 634; the authors warn that LLM results drop on larger code.
  
  **Evidence rows:**
  - RQ1: the CASTLE scores above. (p. 11, V, moderate)
  - RQ1: LLM precision/recall: o3-mini 63%/78%, GPT-4o 54%/76%, R1 47%/90%; small open models have 20–28% precision. (V, weak)
  - RQ1: CodeQL finds 29% (45/150) vs a 23% SAST average; Clang 87%/9% and CBMC 100%/12% precision/recall. (p. 11–12, V, moderate)
  - RQ1: Splint and CodeThreat report more than 1,000 false positives each. (V, moderate)
  - RQ2: benchmark design (single-file, balanced, line-labelled). (p. 6, V, strong)
  - RQ2: TP+FN exceeds the 150 vulnerable programs for most LLMs. (p. 11, I, moderate)
  - RQ3: ESBMC + CodeQL scores 814 (+23%); no LLM+tool hybrid is tested. (p. 13, V, weak)
  - RQ3: reasoning models produce fewer false positives. (V, weak)
  - RQ4: formal verification misses SQLi, path traversal and credentials; no per-CWE numbers are given. (p. 12, A)
  - RQ4: on a 400+ line file, LLM false positives rise and most models miss the hidden bug. (p. 14, A, no numbers)
  - RQ5: scalability, localisation and benchmark overfitting. (A)
  
  **Problems found:**
  - Table 3 counts don't add up: GPT-4o has 136 TP + 43 FN = 179 and R1 has 165 against 150 vulnerable programs. CodeQL (157), Semgrep, GitLab and Jit also exceed 150. Recall and accuracy therefore use inconsistent denominators.
  - The text gives conflicting tool counts: "11 static and 11 LLMs" on p. 3 vs 13+2+10.
  - LLM line-number offsets were corrected using the code line they returned; SAST tools got no such help. The prompt also tells models how they will be scored.
  - The CASTLE Score's weights are the authors' own and are not checked against anything external.
  - The authors filed ESBMC bug reports and earlier work by co-authors used ESBMC; ESBMC tops the non-LLM tools.
  
  ## Across the four papers
  - None of them actually tests an LLM+SAST hybrid, though all recommend one, so the RQ3 evidence is opinion only.
  - The direction of the result depends on code size and setup:
    - Small or synthetic snippets favour LLMs (gnieciak2025large, dubniczky2025castle).
    - Whole real repositories give LLMs high detection but very noisy output (zhou2024comparison).
    - CodeQL still wins on Juliet and OWASP (khare2025understanding).

## gnieciak2025large · ready · full-text (arXiv v1; published in IEEE Access 2025)
**Summary:** Compares SonarQube, CodeQL and Snyk Code (default settings) with zero-shot GPT-4.1, Mistral Large and DeepSeek V3 on 10 small C# projects with 63 vulnerabilities. Mean F1 is 0.797/0.753/0.750 for the LLMs vs 0.260/0.386/0.546 for the SAST tools; LLMs always give the wrong line or column and invent "outdated dependency" findings.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: mean F1 as above. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ1: mean recall is 0.78–0.88 for LLMs vs 0.19–0.52 for SAST; mean precision is 0.72–0.78 vs 0.57–0.69. (p. 10, V, weak)
- RQ1: pooling the raw counts (my arithmetic) gives SAST precision 0.81–0.87 vs LLM 0.74–0.79, and Snyk F1 about 0.70. (p. 8, I, weak)
- RQ2: LLMs get credit for findings at the wrong location; each tool ran once; projects were written by the authors. (p. 5–6, 8, V, moderate)
- RQ3: runtime per project is about 186–213 s for CodeQL, 14–29 s for Snyk and 3.5–67 s for the LLMs. (p. 9, V, weak)
- RQ3: authors recommend LLMs for early triage and SAST for audits, but test no hybrid. (A)
- RQ4: covers only C# SQLi, XSS, secrets, command injection, weak crypto and outdated dependencies, with no per-category results. (V, weak)
- RQ5: open problems are localisation and hallucinated findings. (p. 11–12, A)

**Problems found:**
- The abstract calls the projects "real-world", but the methods say they were "prepared" with "a random number of vulnerabilities" and are 3–5k characters each, which points to seeded test code.
- LLMs are credited for findings at the wrong line or column; SAST tools get no such allowance.
- When a tool reports nothing on a project, its precision is set to 0 and still averaged in, which drags SAST precision down.
- Pooled counts change the false-positive picture: GPT-4.1 has the most false positives (19), not DeepSeek. Snyk's share of false reports (15/57) is about the same as the LLMs'.
- The abstract mentions developer effort and a thematic analysis; neither is reported.
- Temperature, model versions and run cost are not reported. The paper refers to itself as "this thesis".

## khare2025understanding · ready · full-text (arXiv v3; published at ICST 2025)
**Summary:** Tests 16 LLMs with 3 prompts on 5,000 balanced single-function samples (OWASP, Juliet Java and C/C++, CVEFixes Java and C/C++; 25 CWEs). Compares them with CodeQL on the synthetic sets only, and with DeepDFA and LineVul on CVEFixes C/C++. The best LLM averages 62.8% accuracy; CodeQL beats the best LLM on accuracy on all synthetic sets, while LLMs win on specific CWEs.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: best LLM averages 62.8% accuracy; real-world accuracy is 10.5% lower than synthetic. (p. 5, V, moderate)
- RQ1: CodeQL vs best LLM, accuracy/F1: OWASP 0.63/0.72 vs 0.60/0.65; Juliet Java 0.94/0.94 vs 0.76/0.79; Juliet C/C++ 0.72/0.61 vs 0.65/0.72. (p. 9, V, moderate)
- RQ1: on CVEFixes C/C++, Qwen-2.5-32B has F1 0.65 vs DeepDFA 0.23 and LineVul 0.61 (both trained on the same dataset); LineVul trained on BigVul drops to F1 0.02. (p. 10, V, moderate)
- RQ1: larger models are not reliably better. (p. 5, A)
- RQ2: many configurations answer "vulnerable" every time (precision 0.50, recall 1.00, F1 0.67), which is the trivial result on a 50/50 set. (p. 16, I, moderate)
- RQ2: CodeQL is run on synthetic data only, and the best LLM is picked after seeing results from 48 configurations. (V, moderate)
- RQ3: a dataflow-style prompt raises real-world F1 by up to 0.18; sources and sinks are correct in 16–18 of 20 checked samples. (p. 5–6, V, weak)
- RQ3: authors propose LLMs finding sources/sinks for a static analyser to reason over. (A)
- RQ4: LLMs beat CodeQL on CWE-22, 78, 476 and 416 (up to +24%); CodeQL is better on CWE-190 (+11–21%). (p. 8, V, moderate)
- RQ4: LLMs do well on self-contained CWEs and poorly on context-dependent ones (CWE-862, C/C++ out-of-bounds). (p. 7, V, moderate)
- RQ5: missing global context is the main failure cause. (p. 7, A)

**Problems found:**
- The headline F1 of 0.71 is barely above the always-"vulnerable" result of 0.67.
- The abstract says LLMs beat CodeQL; that holds only for certain CWEs, not overall.
- Table V lists DSCoder-15B with a size of "33B".
- The appendix wording on CVEFixes labels reads as reversed.
- No cost data, and no code or data link in this version.

## dubniczky2025castle · ready · full-text (arXiv v2; published as an LNCS chapter, venue_kind "book"; metadata has no abstract)
**Summary:** Introduces CASTLE, 250 hand-written single-file C programs (mean 42 lines, 25 CWEs, 150 vulnerable and 100 clean). Evaluates 13 static analysers, 2 formal verification tools and 10 LLMs using a new author-defined CASTLE Score. GPT-o3-mini scores 977, o1 962, R1 956 and GPT-4o 954, vs ESBMC 661 and CodeQL 634; the authors warn that LLM results drop on larger code.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1: the CASTLE scores above. (p. 11, V, moderate)
- RQ1: LLM precision/recall: o3-mini 63%/78%, GPT-4o 54%/76%, R1 47%/90%; small open models have 20–28% precision. (V, weak)
- RQ1: CodeQL finds 29% (45/150) vs a 23% SAST average; Clang 87%/9% and CBMC 100%/12% precision/recall. (p. 11–12, V, moderate)
- RQ1: Splint and CodeThreat report more than 1,000 false positives each. (V, moderate)
- RQ2: benchmark design (single-file, balanced, line-labelled). (p. 6, V, strong)
- RQ2: TP+FN exceeds the 150 vulnerable programs for most LLMs. (p. 11, I, moderate)
- RQ3: ESBMC + CodeQL scores 814 (+23%); no LLM+tool hybrid is tested. (p. 13, V, weak)
- RQ3: reasoning models produce fewer false positives. (V, weak)
- RQ4: formal verification misses SQLi, path traversal and credentials; no per-CWE numbers are given. (p. 12, A)
- RQ4: on a 400+ line file, LLM false positives rise and most models miss the hidden bug. (p. 14, A, no numbers)
- RQ5: scalability, localisation and benchmark overfitting. (A)

**Problems found:**
- Table 3 counts don't add up: GPT-4o has 136 TP + 43 FN = 179 and R1 has 165 against 150 vulnerable programs. CodeQL (157), Semgrep, GitLab and Jit also exceed 150. Recall and accuracy therefore use inconsistent denominators.
- The text gives conflicting tool counts: "11 static and 11 LLMs" on p. 3 vs 13+2+10.
- LLM line-number offsets were corrected using the code line they returned; SAST tools got no such help. The prompt also tells models how they will be scored.
- The CASTLE Score's weights are the authors' own and are not checked against anything external.
- The authors filed ESBMC bug reports and earlier work by co-authors used ESBMC; ESBMC tops the non-LLM tools.

## Across the four papers
- None of them actually tests an LLM+SAST hybrid, though all recommend one, so the RQ3 evidence is opinion only.
- The direction of the result depends on code size and setup:
  - Small or synthetic snippets favour LLMs (gnieciak2025large, dubniczky2025castle).
  - Whole real repositories give LLMs high detection but very noisy output (zhou2024comparison).
  - CodeQL still wins on Juliet and OWASP (khare2025understanding).

  This is a candidate entry for the RQ2 contradiction section.

  ### kaniewski2026systematic · ready · full-text (arXiv 2507.22659v2, 19 Dec 2025; published in TOSEM 2026)
  **Summary:** A systematic review of 263 studies (Jan 2020–Nov 2025; 185 peer-reviewed, 78 arXiv), searched in IEEE Xplore, ACM DL and arXiv. It gives a detailed classification scheme and recomputes statistics for 20 widely used datasets (class balance, CWE coverage). It maps the field but pools no performance numbers. Its main finding: work is mostly binary, function-level C/C++ classification on noisy, leakage-prone, long-tailed datasets with inconsistent splits, so studies can't be compared.
  
  | RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | RQ1 | No effectiveness synthesis; SAST is described as rule-dependent with high false positives, LLMs as rule-free but unproven outside curated benchmarks | 1, 12–13, 40 | A | weak |
  | RQ2 | Most-used benchmarks are old function-level C/C++ sets (Devign 69 studies, Big-Vul 63, ReVeal 40); vulnerable share ranges 0.7–50% | 26, 28 | V | strong |
  | RQ2 | 87 studies use custom datasets; only 9 datasets are reused in more than 10 studies; few have fixed train/test splits | 35, 39 | V | strong |
  | RQ2 | Popular benchmarks are likely in LLM pre-training data, so scores may reflect memorisation | 30, 38–39 | A | moderate |
  | RQ3 | Static-analysis output is used as LLM input, or the LLM refines its findings; studies that only post-process tool output are excluded | 7–8, 14, 18 | V | moderate |
  | RQ3 | Recommends SAST + LLM pipelines in both directions as the path to industry use (not quantified) | 42 | A | weak |
  | RQ4 | Datasets are C/C++-biased and long-tailed (top-25 CWEs ≈ 80% of labels); 555 usable CWEs appear in no analysed dataset | 28, 32, 34 | V | strong |
  | RQ5 | Seven open-problem themes (L1–L7): granularity, labels and leakage, comparability, outdated knowledge, robustness, explainability, workflow integration and cost | 37–40 | A | strong |
  | RQ5 | Few realistic-setting evaluations; models underperform outside curated benchmarks | 39–40 | A | moderate |
  
  **Open challenges it states:**
  - Repo-level and multilingual benchmarks.
  - Labels checked by hand.
  - Datasets created after model training cutoffs.
  - Fixed splits and documented preprocessing.
  - RAG and continual learning to stay current.
  - Structure-aware, robustness-tested inputs.
  - Metrics for how trustworthy explanations are.
  - Integration into IDEs and CI, and lightweight on-premise models.
  
  **Surprising:** the review excludes studies where the LLM only processes SAST output, yet recommends exactly that pipeline. Evidence for RQ3 hybrids must come from primary studies such as `du2026reducing`, `xiong2026sifting` and `li2024iris`. Its quality assessment gives no scoring scheme, and screening counts per stage are missing. It counts BERT and CodeBERT as LLMs, which blurs our line between LLMs and older deep-learning detectors.
  
  ### zhou2025large · ready · full-text (arXiv 2404.02525v3; published in TOSEM 2025)
  **Summary:** A systematic review of 58 studies on LLMs for vulnerability detection and repair (Jan 2018–Mar 2024): 7 databases plus 17 top venues, with a 0–3 quality score per criterion and a cutoff of 12. As of early 2024, detection was dominated by fine-tuned small encoder models (CodeBERT is 26.1% of uses) on function-level, heuristically labelled data, and no study was built into a developer workflow.
  
  | RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | RQ1 | Only one study in the corpus compares LLMs with SAST: SAST finds fewer vulnerabilities with few false positives, LLMs find more with many false positives | 18, 22 | A | weak |
  | RQ2 | Detection is mostly function-level (7 line-level, 0 class-level, 1 repo-level) | 17–18 | V | moderate |
  | RQ2 | Labels mostly come from vulnerability-fixing commits, which prior work found noisy | 18 | A | moderate |
  | RQ2 | Benchmarks may overlap with pre-training data; contamination-free benchmarks are needed | 20 | A | moderate |
  | RQ4 | LLMs struggle with rare CWEs and with vulnerabilities spanning several functions | 20 | A | weak |
  | RQ5 | A high-quality detection benchmark is still missing; proposes a small, hand-checked, maintained test set | 19, 22 | A | moderate |
  | RQ5 | None of the 58 studies is integrated into a developer workflow | 19 | V | moderate |
  | RQ5 | Repo-level detection, agents, tool use and vulnerability-specific LLMs were under-explored | 22–23 | A | moderate |
  
  **Open challenges it states:** a curated test set; repo-level detection with long-context models; agents and tool use; open vulnerability-specific LLMs; explanations and IDE integration; robustness and accuracy (cites state of the art as 67.6% for detection and 20% for repair).
  
  **Surprising:** its only SAST-vs-LLM evidence is the authors' own study, which is our `zhou2024comparison`. Cite the primary study instead. Studies using only graph or recurrent neural networks are excluded, so it cannot compare LLMs with older deep-learning detectors. The corpus is dated (ends March 2024).
  
  ### sheng2025llms · ready · full-text (arXiv 2502.07049v2, Feb 2025; published in ACM Computing Surveys 2025)
  **Summary:** A narrative survey, not a systematic one: 58 studies drawn from about 500–600 screened (2019–2024), with no database list, search string or quality assessment. It catalogues 42 datasets and lists the key challenges: snippet-only scope, cross-file context, data leakage and label quality, robustness and inconsistent explanations.
  
  | RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | RQ1 | No quantified comparison; says LLMs typically assist static analysis or fuzzing rather than working alone | 20 | A | weak |
  | RQ2 | About 40 studies ("83%") test isolated snippets, which overstates real-world performance | 20 | A | weak |
  | RQ2 | Datasets are narrow, mislabelled and leaky; only 2 of 42 catalogued datasets are repository-level | 3, 13, 25 | A | moderate |
  | RQ2 | Scores depend heavily on the benchmark (CodeBERT 0.099 F1 on PrimeVul vs 0.66 on Choi2017) | 19 | A | weak |
  | RQ3 | 41.3% of studies add code-structure inputs, with modest gains that shrink for cross-file bugs | 16 | V | weak |
  | RQ3 | Combining CodeQL-style analysers with LLMs looks promising but needs better data-flow tracking and efficiency | 3 | A | weak |
  | RQ4 | Studies target C/C++ 50%, Java 21.1%, Solidity 11.8%; memory bugs are detected better than logic bugs | 3, 11 | V | weak |
  | RQ5 | Open challenges: narrow problem scope, complex semantics, robustness and explanations, datasets | 20–25 | A | moderate |
  
  **Open challenges it states:** full-repository and per-commit detection; reproducing vulnerabilities to cut false positives; CWE-specific detection; repository-level datasets with leakage controls; fine-tuning frontier models; ensembles to reduce false positives.
  
  **Doubtful:**
  - **Inconsistent counts:**
    - 56 vs 58 papers.
    - "40 = 83%" implies about 48 papers, not 58.
    - Minimum fine-tuning set given as 10K (p. 19) and as 100K (p. 24).
    - Encoder models "72.4%" vs decoder-only models 67.1% of use; I couldn't reconcile these.
  - **Metric error:** precision is described as "true positive rate", which is recall.
  - **Likely wrong citation:** the CWE-787 vs CWE-862 contrast is cited to [36], which is a 2021 repair paper (probably meant [37]). Don't reuse it unchecked.
  - **Not comparable:** Table 5 sets F1 scores from different datasets side by side.
  
  ### Across all three

  # To Think or Not to Think: Evaluating LLM Reasoning and Agents in Vulnerability Detection
  
  - Authors: Tan, Hua Beng; Widyasari, Ratnadira; Astekin, Merve; Goknil, Arda; Sözer, Hasan; Tun, Yan Naing; Husom, Erik Johannes; Shar, Lwin Khin; Jiang, Lingxiao
  - Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
  - DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837521 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837521

  ## 1. Research objective
  Separate the effects of reasoning-enabled ("thinking") inference, agentic orchestration and explanation quality on LLM vulnerability detection, which prior work examined separately or under heterogeneous settings [A] (p. 1, p. 2).
  
  ## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
  - RQ1: Do reasoning-enabled LLMs outperform non-reasoning LLMs in software vulnerability detection? [V] (p. 2)
  - RQ2: How do multi-agent configurations compare with single-agent setups in performance, cross-setting stability and improvement consistency? [V] (p. 2)
  - RQ3: How does explanation quality differ between thinking and non-thinking LLMs? [V] (p. 2)
  - No formal hypotheses.
  
  ## 3. Methodology
  - Research design: controlled, factor-separated (factorial) experiment. RQ1: 4 models × 2 modes × 2 prompting strategies, non-agent = 16 configurations; RQ2: same × 3 agent designs = 48 configurations; RQ3 on the generated outputs [V] (p. 3, Table 1). Additional call-matched and role-sensitivity experiments (p. 10, p. 11).
  - Approach / model / intervention: Nemotron-Nano-8B, Nemotron-Super-49B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, each in instruct and thinking mode [V] (p. 3, p. 4). Designs: NA (direct call, no state); SA (one agent); DA (Code Author proposes, Security Analyst reviews and decides); MA (Security Researcher, Code Author, Moderator, Review Board) [V] (p. 4). Zero-shot and few-shot prompts with identical structure and examples across models/modes [V] (p. 4).
  - Baselines or comparison conditions: instruct mode vs thinking mode; SA as the agentic baseline; call-matched self-revision with 2 and 4 calls, best-of-4 at T = 0.7, and VulAgent-lite (a specialist hypothesis–validation workflow without Joern CFG/DFG) [V] (p. 10, p. 11). No SAST tools, no fine-tuned deep-learning detectors, no proprietary LLMs as detectors.
  
  ## 4. Dataset and sample
  - Data source(s): PrimeVul Pair; each vulnerable function paired with a benign counterpart sharing ≥80% of its string content; the counterpart is not shown at inference [V] (p. 3, p. 5).
  - Sample size (N) and unit: 870 functions (435 vulnerable, 435 benign) per configuration [V] (p. 3); call-matched experiments on a pair-preserving 193-pair subset, 2 largest models, zero-shot [V] (p. 11). RQ3: 120 explanations (60 snippets × 2 modes, 15 per TP/TN/FP/FN) rated by 2 blinded humans; paired tests on 59 pairs; LLM judge on a 480-explanation frame (2 models × 2 modes × 4 strata × 30) [V] (p. 5, p. 9).
  - Sampling / selection method: full PrimeVul Pair set for RQ1/RQ2; how the 193-pair subset was chosen is not reported beyond "pair-preserving" (p. 11). No power analysis.
  - Data availability (public? link?): replication package with code, prompts and dataset on Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21401826 [V] (p. 5, p. 12).
  
  ## 5. Experimental setup
  - Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: vLLM v0.17–v0.18, 64K context window, NVIDIA H100 80GB on RunPod; temperature 0; pilot repetitions showed no variation, so one run per configuration [V] (p. 4). Agents built with the AG2 framework [V] (p. 4). Outputs auto-parsed to binary labels; non-conforming outputs "handled conservatively" (exact rule not reported) [V] (p. 5). LLM judge: Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 24 few-shot exemplars from held-out human ratings, validated by 5-fold cross-validation against the inter-human agreement level; Claude Opus 4.8 tried as an alternative [V] (p. 5, p. 9). Cost assumes RunPod H100 SXM at $2.69/GPU-hour [V] (p. 10).
  - Code availability: yes, Zenodo package (p. 12).
  
  ## 6. Evaluation metrics
  - Metric — what it measures — why chosen: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (directly interpretable because the data are balanced); P-C, the share of pairs where both functions are classified correctly, to measure discrimination between near-identical code (following Ding et al.) [V] (p. 5). Alert burden: false-positive rate and predicted-positive rate [V] (p. 7). Stability: mean F1, SD and coefficient of variation across settings; improvement consistency = share of matched settings beating SA [V] (p. 5). Explanations: completeness, informativeness, clarity, actionability on 1–5 Likert scales [V] (p. 5). Cost: GPU-hours, kWh, input/output tokens, USD [V] (p. 10).
  - Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilcoxon signed-rank with Cohen's d for RQ1/RQ2 [V] (p. 6, p. 7); Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni for paired explanation scores, Mann–Whitney for correct vs incorrect, Spearman and partial Spearman for length effects [V] (p. 5, p. 8, p. 9). No confidence intervals reported; the reasoning × orchestration interaction is not significance-tested [A] (p. 8).
  
  ## 7. Key findings
  1. Non-agent: thinking beats instruct F1 in 7 of 8 model–prompt settings; mean F1 0.31 → 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37); accuracy barely changes (0.518 vs 0.523, p = 0.46), so the gain is a recall shift — [V] (p. 6).
  2. Best non-agent F1: Nemotron-Super-49B thinking zero-shot F1 0.620 (recall 0.749, precision 0.529); best non-agent P-C: Qwen3-30B-A3B instruct zero-shot 22.5% — [V] (p. 6, Table 2). Nemotron-Nano-8B stays weak (zero-shot recall 0.005–0.048) — [V] (p. 6).
  3. Thinking improves P-C in 6 of 8 non-agent settings — [V] (p. 6).
  4. Agent designs (means over 16 settings): SA F1 0.368 / recall 0.326 / P-C 13.7; DA F1 0.634 / recall 0.885 / precision 0.502 / P-C 6.2; MA F1 0.497 / recall 0.559 / P-C 15.8 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
  5. DA flags 88.2% of functions (PPR 0.882, FPR 0.880) vs SA 30.3% (FPR 0.280) and MA 55.4% (FPR 0.549); DA vs SA F1 p < 0.0001, d = 1.40; MA vs SA p = 0.0013, d = 0.92 — [V] (p. 7).
  6. DA beats SA on F1 in all 16 settings and is the most stable (CV 9% vs MA 32%, SA 46%); MA has the best P-C in 11 of 16 settings, DA in none — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
  7. Thinking's F1 benefit reverses with orchestration: ΔF1 +0.104 (NA), +0.100 (SA), −0.054 (DA), −0.066 (MA); ΔP-C stays positive (+1.9, +1.5, +8.1, +5.4) — [V] (p. 8, Table 5).
  8. Call-matched (193 pairs, zero-shot, 2 models): 4-call self-revision has the highest mean P-C (24.7) vs SA and MA (21.9) and DA (4.7), with FPR 0.47 vs DA 0.93; the authors conclude much of the multi-agent benefit is extra inference budget — [V]/[A] (p. 11, Table 9).
  9. Cost: thinking uses 2.7–4.4× more energy and 2.5–3.6× more output tokens; MA-thinking averages 25,533 tokens per sample vs 3,703 for NA; per configuration SA $27.5 / 8.0 h, DA $37.1 / 11.5 h, MA $52.7 / 14.4 h; all 64 configurations cost about $2,448, 481 kWh and 423.0M tokens — [V] (p. 10, Table 8).
  10. Explanations (Nemotron-Super-49B, 59 pairs): the LLM judge rates thinking higher on completeness (+0.49), clarity (+0.51) and informativeness (+0.64); humans corroborate only informativeness (+0.30, p = 0.006) — [V] (p. 8).
  11. Thinking explanations are 4.6× longer (13,579 vs 2,935 chars); controlling for length shrinks the judge's mode effect by about 40–60% but does not remove it; for Qwen3-30B no thinking advantage — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).
  12. Blinded explanation quality does not differ between correct and incorrect predictions (e.g. completeness 3.58 vs 3.61, all Mann–Whitney p > 0.3); an unblinded judge creates a spurious gap (3.51 vs 2.22) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).
  
  ## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
  - [A] Deterministic decoding (T = 0) and a single run per configuration: results limited to deterministic decoding, no repeated-run variability (p. 11).
  - [A] Prompt sensitivity and agent-design choices; configurations are representative, not task-optimal (p. 11).
  - [A] Metrics may not fully capture the constructs; the rubric measures developer-facing quality, not faithfulness; a single external Claude judge may have stylistic and length preferences (p. 11).
  - [A] Function-level PrimeVul Pair only; no project context, interprocedural reasoning or repository-level vulnerabilities; only four open Nemotron/Qwen models, larger models (DeepSeek-V3.1, Kimi-K2) not run due to hardware budget (p. 3, p. 11).
  - [A] RQ3 manual evaluation uses a sample, which adds sampling uncertainty (p. 11).
  - [A] The call-matched results are single runs and reported descriptively (p. 11).
  
  ## 9. Limitations we identified
  - [I] An "always vulnerable" classifier scores F1 = 0.667 on this balanced set (precision 0.5, recall 1.0). No reported configuration exceeds it (Table 3 max 0.665, Table 9 max 0.666), so DA's "highest F1" is near the trivial flag-everything point. Based on Table 3 (p. 7) and Table 9 (p. 11).
  - [I] All P-C values are ≤26.9%, close to the 25% expected from random independent labelling of each pair member, so absolute discrimination is weak in every design. Based on Tables 2, 4 and 9 (p. 6, p. 7, p. 11).
  - [I] No SAST or deep-learning baselines, so the paper says nothing about LLMs vs traditional tools. Based on Table 1 (p. 3).
  - [I] Training-data contamination is not discussed; PrimeVul is public and the open models may have seen it. Based on a search of the full text for contamination or memorisation (none found).
  - [I] Statistical tests on 8 or 16 paired configuration-level means have little power and no correction across RQ1/RQ2 tests; differences between individual cells should not be over-read (the authors say this too, p. 6).
  - [I] Wording conflict: the abstract and conclusion say explanation gains are "largely" length-mediated (p. 11), while Section 4.3 says "substantially but not wholly" (40–60%) (p. 9).
  - [I] Selection of the 193-pair subset and the handling of non-conforming outputs are not described, which limits checks on Table 9. Based on p. 5, p. 11.
  
  ## 10. Threats to validity
  - Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): agent designs differ in number of calls and context, partly controlled by call-matched baselines (p. 7, p. 11); possible pretraining contamination not addressed; parsing rule for non-conforming outputs unspecified (p. 5).
  - External (generalisability of sample/context): function-level C/C++, one benchmark, four mid-size open models (p. 11).
  - Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): F1 on balanced data rewards over-flagging (authors pair it with P-C, p. 7); explanation rubric measures perceived quality, not faithfulness (p. 11).
  - Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single runs; small numbers of paired configuration means; Bonferroni applied only in RQ3 (p. 8, p. 9).
  - Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — open models, vLLM versions, hardware, prompts and replication package on Zenodo (p. 4, p. 12).
  
  ## 11. Future research directions
  - Stated by authors [A]: more reasoning-oriented families (distilled DeepSeek-R1, Gemma) and larger models; costlier repository-level settings with dependency resolution, retrieval and tool support (p. 11); deeper per-model analysis and significance testing of the reasoning × orchestration interaction (p. 8).
  - Suggested by us [I]: report the trivial flag-all and random baselines alongside F1/P-C; add SAST and fine-tuned DL baselines on the same pairs; repeat runs with non-zero temperature for variance.
  
  ## 12. Relevance to our research
  - Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM-only variants), RQ2, RQ3, RQ5.
  - How it informs our work [I]: controlled evidence that reasoning modes and multi-agent designs mainly shift the recall/false-positive trade-off rather than improving discrimination, with detailed energy, token and USD costs. Useful for RQ3 (cost vs benefit of agentic LLM designs) and RQ2 (F1 vs pairwise metrics), and consistent with yildiz2025benchmarking's finding that F1 hides near-random pairwise accuracy. No traditional or DL baseline, so it does not inform LLM-vs-SAST directly.

  | RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |

  | RQ1 | Thinking mode raises non-agent mean F1 from 0.31 to 0.41 across 4 open models (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, d = 1.37), mainly via recall; accuracy unchanged (0.518 vs 0.523) | p. 6 | V | moderate |

  | RQ3 | Thinking's F1 benefit turns negative under DA (−0.054) and MA (−0.066) | p. 8 | V | weak |
  | RQ5 | Blinded explanation quality is indistinguishable between correct and incorrect predictions (all p > 0.3); fluent explanations do not signal correctness | p. 9 | V | moderate |

  - RQ1: Do reasoning-enabled LLMs outperform non-reasoning LLMs in software vulnerability detection? [V] (p. 2)
  - RQ2: How do multi-agent configurations compare with single-agent setups in performance, cross-setting stability and improvement consistency? [V] (p. 2)
  - RQ3: How does explanation quality differ between thinking and non-thinking LLMs? [V] (p. 2)
  - No formal hypotheses.
  
  ## 3. Methodology
  - Research design: controlled, factor-separated (factorial) experiment. RQ1: 4 models × 2 modes × 2 prompting strategies, non-agent = 16 configurations; RQ2: same × 3 agent designs = 48 configurations; RQ3 on the generated outputs [V] (p. 3, Table 1). Additional call-matched and role-sensitivity experiments (p. 10, p. 11).

RQ3: 120 explanations (60 snippets × 2 modes, 15 per TP/TN/FP/FN) rated by 2 blinded humans; paired tests on 59 pairs; LLM judge on a 480-explanation frame (2 models × 2 modes × 4 strata × 30) [V] (p. 5, p. 9).

Agents built with the AG2 framework [V] (p. 4). Outputs auto-parsed to binary labels; non-conforming outputs "handled conservatively" (exact rule not reported) [V] (p. 5). LLM judge: Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 24 few-shot exemplars from held-out human ratings, validated by 5-fold cross-validation against the inter-human agreement level; Claude Opus 4.8 tried as an alternative [V] (p. 5, p. 9). Cost assumes RunPod H100 SXM at $2.69/GPU-hour [V] (p. 10).
  - Code availability: yes, Zenodo package (p. 12).
  
  ## 6. Evaluation metrics
  - Metric — what it measures — why chosen: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (directly interpretable because the data are balanced); P-C, the share of pairs where both functions are classified correctly, to measure discrimination between near-identical code (following Ding et al.) [V] (p. 5). Alert burden: false-positive rate and predicted-positive rate [V] (p. 7). Stability: mean F1, SD and coefficient of variation across settings; improvement consistency = share of matched settings beating SA [V] (p. 5). Explanations: completeness, informativeness, clarity, actionability on 1–5 Likert scales [V] (p. 5). Cost: GPU-hours, kWh, input/output tokens, USD [V] (p. 10).

No confidence intervals reported; the reasoning × orchestration interaction is not significance-tested [A] (p. 8).

  1. Non-agent: thinking beats instruct F1 in 7 of 8 model–prompt settings; mean F1 0.31 → 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37); accuracy barely changes (0.518 vs 0.523, p = 0.46), so the gain is a recall shift — [V] (p. 6).
  2. Best non-agent F1: Nemotron-Super-49B thinking zero-shot F1 0.620 (recall 0.749, precision 0.529); best non-agent P-C: Qwen3-30B-A3B instruct zero-shot 22.5% — [V] (p. 6, Table 2). Nemotron-Nano-8B stays weak (zero-shot recall 0.005–0.048) — [V] (p. 6).

Cost: thinking uses 2.7–4.4× more energy and 2.5–3.6× more output tokens; MA-thinking averages 25,533 tokens per sample vs 3,703 for NA; per configuration SA $27.5 / 8.0 h, DA $37.1 / 11.5 h, MA $52.7 / 14.4 h; all 64 configurations cost about $2,448, 481 kWh and 423.0M tokens — [V] (p. 10, Table 8).

  - [A] Deterministic decoding (T = 0) and a single run per configuration: results limited to deterministic decoding, no repeated-run variability (p. 11).
  - [A] Prompt sensitivity and agent-design choices; configurations are representative, not task-optimal (p. 11).
  - [A] Metrics may not fully capture the constructs; the rubric measures developer-facing quality, not faithfulness; a single external Claude judge may have stylistic and length preferences (p. 11).

  - Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — open models, vLLM versions, hardware, prompts and replication package on Zenodo (p. 4, p. 12).

  - Stated by authors [A]: more reasoning-oriented families (distilled DeepSeek-R1, Gemma) and larger models; costlier repository-level settings with dependency resolution, retrieval and tool support (p. 11); deeper per-model analysis and significance testing of the reasoning × orchestration interaction (p. 8).

  - Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM-only variants), RQ2, RQ3, RQ5.
