# To Think or Not to Think: Evaluating LLM Reasoning and Agents in Vulnerability Detection

- Authors: Tan, Hua Beng; Widyasari, Ratnadira; Astekin, Merve; Goknil, Arda; Sözer, Hasan; Tun, Yan Naing; Husom, Erik Johannes; Shar, Lwin Khin; Jiang, Lingxiao
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837521 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837521
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` from the user-supplied publisher PDF (ACM version of record, ASE '26, 13 pages, printed pp. 2856–2868; page refs = PDF page index).

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
Separate the effects of reasoning-enabled ("thinking") inference, agentic orchestration and explanation quality on LLM vulnerability detection, which prior work examined separately or under heterogeneous settings [A] (p. 1, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- RQ1: Do reasoning-enabled LLMs outperform non-reasoning LLMs in software vulnerability detection? [V] (p. 2)
- RQ2: How do multi-agent configurations compare with single-agent setups in performance, cross-setting stability and improvement consistency? [V] (p. 2)
- RQ3: How does explanation quality differ between thinking and non-thinking LLMs? [V] (p. 2)
- No formal hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: controlled, factor-separated (factorial) experiment. RQ1: 4 models × 2 modes × 2 prompting strategies, non-agent = 16 configurations; RQ2: same × 3 agent designs = 48 configurations; RQ3 on the generated outputs [V] (p. 3, Table 1). Additional call-matched and role-sensitivity experiments (p. 10, p. 11).
- Approach / model / intervention: Nemotron-Nano-8B, Nemotron-Super-49B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, each in instruct and thinking mode [V] (p. 3, p. 4). Designs: NA (direct call, no state); SA (one agent); DA (Code Author proposes, Security Analyst reviews and decides); MA (Security Researcher, Code Author, Moderator, Review Board) [V] (p. 4). Zero-shot and few-shot prompts with identical structure and examples across models/modes [V] (p. 4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: instruct mode vs thinking mode; SA as the agentic baseline; call-matched self-revision with 2 and 4 calls, best-of-4 at T = 0.7, and VulAgent-lite (a specialist hypothesis–validation workflow without Joern CFG/DFG) [V] (p. 10, p. 11). No SAST tools, no fine-tuned deep-learning detectors, no proprietary LLMs as detectors.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): PrimeVul Pair; each vulnerable function paired with a benign counterpart sharing ≥80% of its string content; the counterpart is not shown at inference [V] (p. 3, p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit: 870 functions (435 vulnerable, 435 benign) per configuration [V] (p. 3); call-matched experiments on a pair-preserving 193-pair subset, 2 largest models, zero-shot [V] (p. 11). RQ3: 120 explanations (60 snippets × 2 modes, 15 per TP/TN/FP/FN) rated by 2 blinded humans; paired tests on 59 pairs; LLM judge on a 480-explanation frame (2 models × 2 modes × 4 strata × 30) [V] (p. 5, p. 9).
- Sampling / selection method: full PrimeVul Pair set for RQ1/RQ2; how the 193-pair subset was chosen is not reported beyond "pair-preserving" (p. 11). No power analysis.
- Data availability (public? link?): replication package with code, prompts and dataset on Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21401826 [V] (p. 5, p. 12).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: vLLM v0.17–v0.18, 64K context window, NVIDIA H100 80GB on RunPod; temperature 0; pilot repetitions showed no variation, so one run per configuration [V] (p. 4). Agents built with the AG2 framework [V] (p. 4). Outputs auto-parsed to binary labels; non-conforming outputs "handled conservatively" (exact rule not reported) [V] (p. 5). LLM judge: Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 24 few-shot exemplars from held-out human ratings, validated by 5-fold cross-validation against the inter-human agreement level; Claude Opus 4.8 tried as an alternative [V] (p. 5, p. 9). Cost assumes RunPod H100 SXM at $2.69/GPU-hour [V] (p. 10).
- Code availability: yes, Zenodo package (p. 12).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (directly interpretable because the data are balanced); P-C, the share of pairs where both functions are classified correctly, to measure discrimination between near-identical code (following Ding et al.) [V] (p. 5). Alert burden: false-positive rate and predicted-positive rate [V] (p. 7). Stability: mean F1, SD and coefficient of variation across settings; improvement consistency = share of matched settings beating SA [V] (p. 5). Explanations: completeness, informativeness, clarity, actionability on 1–5 Likert scales [V] (p. 5). Cost: GPU-hours, kWh, input/output tokens, USD [V] (p. 10).
- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilcoxon signed-rank with Cohen's d for RQ1/RQ2 [V] (p. 6, p. 7); Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni for paired explanation scores, Mann–Whitney for correct vs incorrect, Spearman and partial Spearman for length effects [V] (p. 5, p. 8, p. 9). No confidence intervals reported; the reasoning × orchestration interaction is not significance-tested [A] (p. 8).

## 7. Key findings
1. Non-agent: thinking beats instruct F1 in 7 of 8 model–prompt settings; mean F1 0.31 → 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37); accuracy barely changes (0.518 vs 0.523, p = 0.46), so the gain is a recall shift — [V] (p. 6).
2. Best non-agent F1: Nemotron-Super-49B thinking zero-shot F1 0.620 (recall 0.749, precision 0.529); best non-agent P-C: Qwen3-30B-A3B instruct zero-shot 22.5% — [V] (p. 6, Table 2). Nemotron-Nano-8B stays weak (zero-shot recall 0.005–0.048) — [V] (p. 6).
3. Thinking improves P-C in 6 of 8 non-agent settings — [V] (p. 6).
4. Agent designs (means over 16 settings): SA F1 0.368 / recall 0.326 / P-C 13.7; DA F1 0.634 / recall 0.885 / precision 0.502 / P-C 6.2; MA F1 0.497 / recall 0.559 / P-C 15.8 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
5. DA flags 88.2% of functions (PPR 0.882, FPR 0.880) vs SA 30.3% (FPR 0.280) and MA 55.4% (FPR 0.549); DA vs SA F1 p < 0.0001, d = 1.40; MA vs SA p = 0.0013, d = 0.92 — [V] (p. 7).
6. DA beats SA on F1 in all 16 settings and is the most stable (CV 9% vs MA 32%, SA 46%); MA has the best P-C in 11 of 16 settings, DA in none — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
7. Thinking's F1 benefit reverses with orchestration: ΔF1 +0.104 (NA), +0.100 (SA), −0.054 (DA), −0.066 (MA); ΔP-C stays positive (+1.9, +1.5, +8.1, +5.4) — [V] (p. 8, Table 5).
8. Call-matched (193 pairs, zero-shot, 2 models): 4-call self-revision has the highest mean P-C (24.7) vs SA and MA (21.9) and DA (4.7), with FPR 0.47 vs DA 0.93; the authors conclude much of the multi-agent benefit is extra inference budget — [V]/[A] (p. 11, Table 9).
9. Cost: thinking uses 2.7–4.4× more energy and 2.5–3.6× more output tokens; MA-thinking averages 25,533 tokens per sample vs 3,703 for NA; per configuration SA $27.5 / 8.0 h, DA $37.1 / 11.5 h, MA $52.7 / 14.4 h; all 64 configurations cost about $2,448, 481 kWh and 423.0M tokens — [V] (p. 10, Table 8).
10. Explanations (Nemotron-Super-49B, 59 pairs): the LLM judge rates thinking higher on completeness (+0.49), clarity (+0.51) and informativeness (+0.64); humans corroborate only informativeness (+0.30, p = 0.006) — [V] (p. 8).
11. Thinking explanations are 4.6× longer (13,579 vs 2,935 chars); controlling for length shrinks the judge's mode effect by about 40–60% but does not remove it; for Qwen3-30B no thinking advantage — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).
12. Blinded explanation quality does not differ between correct and incorrect predictions (e.g. completeness 3.58 vs 3.61, all Mann–Whitney p > 0.3); an unblinded judge creates a spurious gap (3.51 vs 2.22) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Deterministic decoding (T = 0) and a single run per configuration: results limited to deterministic decoding, no repeated-run variability (p. 11).
- [A] Prompt sensitivity and agent-design choices; configurations are representative, not task-optimal (p. 11).
- [A] Metrics may not fully capture the constructs; the rubric measures developer-facing quality, not faithfulness; a single external Claude judge may have stylistic and length preferences (p. 11).
- [A] Function-level PrimeVul Pair only; no project context, interprocedural reasoning or repository-level vulnerabilities; only four open Nemotron/Qwen models, larger models (DeepSeek-V3.1, Kimi-K2) not run due to hardware budget (p. 3, p. 11).
- [A] RQ3 manual evaluation uses a sample, which adds sampling uncertainty (p. 11).
- [A] The call-matched results are single runs and reported descriptively (p. 11).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] An "always vulnerable" classifier scores F1 = 0.667 on this balanced set (precision 0.5, recall 1.0). No reported configuration exceeds it (Table 3 max 0.665, Table 9 max 0.666), so DA's "highest F1" is near the trivial flag-everything point. Based on Table 3 (p. 7) and Table 9 (p. 11).
- [I] All P-C values are ≤26.9%, close to the 25% expected from random independent labelling of each pair member, so absolute discrimination is weak in every design. Based on Tables 2, 4 and 9 (p. 6, p. 7, p. 11).
- [I] No SAST or deep-learning baselines, so the paper says nothing about LLMs vs traditional tools. Based on Table 1 (p. 3).
- [I] Training-data contamination is not discussed; PrimeVul is public and the open models may have seen it. Based on a search of the full text for contamination or memorisation (none found).
- [I] Statistical tests on 8 or 16 paired configuration-level means have little power and no correction across RQ1/RQ2 tests; differences between individual cells should not be over-read (the authors say this too, p. 6).
- [I] Wording conflict: the abstract and conclusion say explanation gains are "largely" length-mediated (p. 11), while Section 4.3 says "substantially but not wholly" (40–60%) (p. 9).
- [I] Selection of the 193-pair subset and the handling of non-conforming outputs are not described, which limits checks on Table 9. Based on p. 5, p. 11.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): agent designs differ in number of calls and context, partly controlled by call-matched baselines (p. 7, p. 11); possible pretraining contamination not addressed; parsing rule for non-conforming outputs unspecified (p. 5).
- External (generalisability of sample/context): function-level C/C++, one benchmark, four mid-size open models (p. 11).
- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): F1 on balanced data rewards over-flagging (authors pair it with P-C, p. 7); explanation rubric measures perceived quality, not faithfulness (p. 11).
- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): single runs; small numbers of paired configuration means; Bonferroni applied only in RQ3 (p. 8, p. 9).
- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): good — open models, vLLM versions, hardware, prompts and replication package on Zenodo (p. 4, p. 12).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: more reasoning-oriented families (distilled DeepSeek-R1, Gemma) and larger models; costlier repository-level settings with dependency resolution, retrieval and tool support (p. 11); deeper per-model analysis and significance testing of the reasoning × orchestration interaction (p. 8).
- Suggested by us [I]: report the trivial flag-all and random baselines alongside F1/P-C; add SAST and fine-tuned DL baselines on the same pairs; repeat runs with non-zero temperature for variance.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (LLM-only variants), RQ2, RQ3, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]: controlled evidence that reasoning modes and multi-agent designs mainly shift the recall/false-positive trade-off rather than improving discrimination, with detailed energy, token and USD costs. Useful for RQ3 (cost vs benefit of agentic LLM designs) and RQ2 (F1 vs pairwise metrics), and consistent with yildiz2025benchmarking's finding that F1 hides near-random pairwise accuracy. No traditional or DL baseline, so it does not inform LLM-vs-SAST directly.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | Thinking mode raises non-agent mean F1 from 0.31 to 0.41 across 4 open models (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, d = 1.37), mainly via recall; accuracy unchanged (0.518 vs 0.523) | p. 6 | V | moderate |
| RQ1 | Best function-level F1 on PrimeVul Pair is 0.620 (Nemotron-Super-49B thinking) and best non-agent P-C 22.5%, i.e. weak discrimination of vulnerable vs patched functions | p. 6 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Dual-agent design reaches the highest F1 (0.634) by flagging 88.2% of functions (FPR 0.880) and has the worst pairwise accuracy (P-C 6.2) | p. 7 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | F1 on balanced data and pairwise correctness rank designs differently: MA best on P-C in 11/16 settings, DA in 0/16 despite best F1 | p. 7, p. 8 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Four-call self-revision matches or beats the multi-agent pipeline on P-C (24.7 vs 21.9) on 193 pairs: much of the agent gain is extra inference budget | p. 11 | V | weak |
| RQ3 | Thinking uses 2.7–4.4× more energy and 2.5–3.6× more output tokens; MA-thinking uses ~25.5K tokens per function; per-configuration cost SA $27.5, DA $37.1, MA $52.7 | p. 10 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Thinking's F1 benefit turns negative under DA (−0.054) and MA (−0.066) | p. 8 | V | weak |
| RQ5 | Blinded explanation quality is indistinguishable between correct and incorrect predictions (all p > 0.3); fluent explanations do not signal correctness | p. 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Authors call for repository-level evaluation with dependency resolution, retrieval and tools | p. 11 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "thinking improves mean F1 from 0.31 to 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37)" (p. 6)

> "DA flags 88.2% of functions (PPR = 0.882, FPR = 0.880)" (p. 7)

> "much of the apparent collaboration benefit reflects additional inference budget rather than multi-agent structure itself" (p. 11)

> "the explanation does not reveal its own incorrectness" (p. 9)

## Analyst notes
- Source: publisher version of record (ACM, ASE 2026; Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence; DOI printed on p. 1), supplied by the user and attached with `rlab attach`; identity check "match (DOI printed in PDF)". This replaces the earlier abstract-only analysis.
- Reading coverage: all 13 PDF pages read (pp. 1–11 body, pp. 12–13 acknowledgements, data availability, references). Figures 1–4 (heatmaps and bar charts) are images; their values were taken from Tables 2–9 and the text.
- Uncertainties: the 𝑝 symbol in quotes is rendered as "p" (extraction shows "𝑝"); quote 3 is joined across a hyphenated line break ("col-laboration"). Table 8 prints "36.4,kWh" (typo) (p. 10). Funding: EU Horizon Europe and Research Council of Norway (p. 12); no conflicts of interest declared. Claude Sonnet 4.6 as judge is from a different family from the evaluated models (p. 5).

## 1. Research objective

+Separate the effects of reasoning-enabled ("thinking") inference, agentic orchestration and explanation quality on LLM vulnerability detection, which prior work examined separately or under heterogeneous settings [A] (p. 1, p. 2).
## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
+- RQ1: Do reasoning-enabled LLMs outperform non-reasoning LLMs in software vulnerability detection? [V] (p. 2)
+- RQ2: How do multi-agent configurations compare with single-agent setups in performance, cross-setting stability and improvement consistency? [V] (p. 2)
+- RQ3: How does explanation quality differ between thinking and non-thinking LLMs? [V] (p. 2)
+- No formal hypotheses.
## 3. Methodology
-- Research design:
-- Approach / model / intervention:
-- Baselines or comparison conditions:

+- Research design: controlled, factor-separated (factorial) experiment. RQ1: 4 models × 2 modes × 2 prompting strategies, non-agent = 16 configurations; RQ2: same × 3 agent designs = 48 configurations; RQ3 on the generated outputs [V] (p. 3, Table 1). Additional call-matched and role-sensitivity experiments (p. 10, p. 11).

+- Approach / model / intervention: Nemotron-Nano-8B, Nemotron-Super-49B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, each in instruct and thinking mode [V] (p. 3, p. 4). Designs: NA (direct call, no state); SA (one agent); DA (Code Author proposes, Security Analyst reviews and decides); MA (Security Researcher, Code Author, Moderator, Review Board) [V] (p. 4). Zero-shot and few-shot prompts with identical structure and examples across models/modes [V] (p. 4).

+- Baselines or comparison conditions: instruct mode vs thinking mode; SA as the agentic baseline; call-matched self-revision with 2 and 4 calls, best-of-4 at T = 0.7, and VulAgent-lite (a specialist hypothesis–validation workflow without Joern CFG/DFG) [V] (p. 10, p. 11). No SAST tools, no fine-tuned deep-learning detectors, no proprietary LLMs as detectors.
## 4. Dataset and sample
-- Data source(s):
-- Sample size (N) and unit:
-- Sampling / selection method:
-- Data availability (public? link?):
+- Data source(s): PrimeVul Pair; each vulnerable function paired with a benign counterpart sharing ≥80% of its string content; the counterpart is not shown at inference [V] (p. 3, p. 5).

+- Sample size (N) and unit: 870 functions (435 vulnerable, 435 benign) per configuration [V] (p. 3); call-matched experiments on a pair-preserving 193-pair subset, 2 largest models, zero-shot [V] (p. 11). RQ3: 120 explanations (60 snippets × 2 modes, 15 per TP/TN/FP/FN) rated by 2 blinded humans; paired tests on 59 pairs; LLM judge on a 480-explanation frame (2 models × 2 modes × 4 strata × 30) [V] (p. 5, p. 9).
+- Sampling / selection method: full PrimeVul Pair set for RQ1/RQ2; how the 193-pair subset was chosen is not reported beyond "pair-preserving" (p. 11). No power analysis.
+- Data availability (public? link?): replication package with code, prompts and dataset on Zenodo, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21401826 [V] (p. 5, p. 12).
## 5. Experimental setup
-- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
-- Code availability:

+- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: vLLM v0.17–v0.18, 64K context window, NVIDIA H100 80GB on RunPod; temperature 0; pilot repetitions showed no variation, so one run per configuration [V] (p. 4). Agents built with the AG2 framework [V] (p. 4). Outputs auto-parsed to binary labels; non-conforming outputs "handled conservatively" (exact rule not reported) [V] (p. 5). LLM judge: Claude Sonnet 4.6 with 24 few-shot exemplars from held-out human ratings, validated by 5-fold cross-validation against the inter-human agreement level; Claude Opus 4.8 tried as an alternative [V] (p. 5, p. 9). Cost assumes RunPod H100 SXM at $2.69/GPU-hour [V] (p. 10).
+- Code availability: yes, Zenodo package (p. 12).
## 6. Evaluation metrics
-- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
-- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):

+- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (directly interpretable because the data are balanced); P-C, the share of pairs where both functions are classified correctly, to measure discrimination between near-identical code (following Ding et al.) [V] (p. 5). Alert burden: false-positive rate and predicted-positive rate [V] (p. 7). Stability: mean F1, SD and coefficient of variation across settings; improvement consistency = share of matched settings beating SA [V] (p. 5). Explanations: completeness, informativeness, clarity, actionability on 1–5 Likert scales [V] (p. 5). Cost: GPU-hours, kWh, input/output tokens, USD [V] (p. 10).

+- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): Wilcoxon signed-rank with Cohen's d for RQ1/RQ2 [V] (p. 6, p. 7); Wilcoxon signed-rank with Bonferroni for paired explanation scores, Mann–Whitney for correct vs incorrect, Spearman and partial Spearman for length effects [V] (p. 5, p. 8, p. 9). No confidence intervals reported; the reasoning × orchestration interaction is not significance-tested [A] (p. 8).
## 7. Key findings
-1. finding — numbers — [V]/[A] (p. N)

+1. Non-agent: thinking beats instruct F1 in 7 of 8 model–prompt settings; mean F1 0.31 → 0.41 (Wilcoxon p = 0.023, Cohen's d = 1.37); accuracy barely changes (0.518 vs 0.523, p = 0.46), so the gain is a recall shift — [V] (p. 6).

+2. Best non-agent F1: Nemotron-Super-49B thinking zero-shot F1 0.620 (recall 0.749, precision 0.529); best non-agent P-C: Qwen3-30B-A3B instruct zero-shot 22.5% — [V] (p. 6, Table 2). Nemotron-Nano-8B stays weak (zero-shot recall 0.005–0.048) — [V] (p. 6).
+3. Thinking improves P-C in 6 of 8 non-agent settings — [V] (p. 6).
+4. Agent designs (means over 16 settings): SA F1 0.368 / recall 0.326 / P-C 13.7; DA F1 0.634 / recall 0.885 / precision 0.502 / P-C 6.2; MA F1 0.497 / recall 0.559 / P-C 15.8 — [V] (p. 7, Table 3).
+5. DA flags 88.2% of functions (PPR 0.882, FPR 0.880) vs SA 30.3% (FPR 0.280) and MA 55.4% (FPR 0.549); DA vs SA F1 p < 0.0001, d = 1.40; MA vs SA p = 0.0013, d = 0.92 — [V] (p. 7).
+6. DA beats SA on F1 in all 16 settings and is the most stable (CV 9% vs MA 32%, SA 46%); MA has the best P-C in 11 of 16 settings, DA in none — [V] (p. 7, p. 8).
+7. Thinking's F1 benefit reverses with orchestration: ΔF1 +0.104 (NA), +0.100 (SA), −0.054 (DA), −0.066 (MA); ΔP-C stays positive (+1.9, +1.5, +8.1, +5.4) — [V] (p. 8, Table 5).

+8. Call-matched (193 pairs, zero-shot, 2 models): 4-call self-revision has the highest mean P-C (24.7) vs SA and MA (21.9) and DA (4.7), with FPR 0.47 vs DA 0.93; the authors conclude much of the multi-agent benefit is extra inference budget — [V]/[A] (p. 11, Table 9).

+9. +- [I] An "always vulnerable" classifier scores F1 = 0.667 on this balanced set (precision 0.5, recall 1.0). No reported configuration exceeds it (Table 3 max 0.665, Table 9 max 0.666), so DA's "highest F1" is near the trivial flag-everything point. Based on Table 3 (p. 7) and Table 9 (p. 11).

content.text:
The analysis phase is finished: all 20 papers are analysed from their full text, and the citation check passed on every file.

**What the 20 analyses show so far:**
1. **Who wins depends on the setup.** On small or synthetic code, LLMs look better than SAST. On standard test suites such as Juliet and OWASP, CodeQL is still ahead. On whole real repositories, LLMs find a lot but also raise a lot of false alarms.
2. **Older benchmarks are unreliable.** In them, only 24–60% of the "vulnerable" labels are correct, and up to 19% of test samples are exact copies of training data. On realistic data, F1 drops from about 68% to about 2–21%.
3. **High F1 can be misleading.** Several LLM setups score high F1 mostly by labelling nearly everything vulnerable. When a test checks whether the model can tell a vulnerable function from its fixed version, it does close to random guessing.
4. **Contradictions:** RepoAudit's own paper reports 78% precision, but an independent study (TSE 2026) found 0–6% recall on overlapping projects. And a 2023 ChatGPT study disagrees with a 2025 PrimeVul study about whether fine-tuned models or GPT-4 do better.
5. **Possible gap:** many papers recommend combining LLMs with SAST, but few test it fairly. No study compares LLMs, SAST and deep learning on the same cleaned benchmark. This needs a novelty check before we can claim it as a gap.

Four of the analyses couldn't be saved by their agents because of a harness restriction, so I saved them myself. I also checked their key numbers against the paper text.

**Now running:** 2 reviewers are checking all 20 analyses against the original papers (wrong page references, mislabelled claims, arithmetic). Any problems they find go back for fixing. After that come the synthesis, the gap analysis and the report.

  5. **Related evidence, not duplicated data:** guo and li share five projects at different commits; ahmed and khare both draw on NVD/CVEFixes-style C/C++ fix commits; yildiz and tan both use PrimeVul.
  6. **Source versions:** six analyses use arXiv text of published papers, and guo is camera-ready text registered as a preprint. All record this, but numbers should be re-checked against the versions of record before the final report.

description: Compare methodologies, datasets, metrics and findings across a project's analysed papers, consolidate the evidence matrix and identify contradictions. Use after paper analyses are complete, or when the user asks how studies differ or agree.
---

# Compare methodologies

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) §1, §5, §6.

Input: project id. Use only analyses with `status: ready` or `complete`; `rlab index <id>` then read `literature-matrix.md` for the overview, and each `papers/*/analysis.md` for detail.

## 1. Evidence matrix
Merge every analysis's evidence table (section 13) into `evidence-matrix.md`, one row per claim, Source as `[@key, p. N]`. Keep the paper's label; downgrade strength for abstract-only and preprint sources.

## 2. Methodology comparison
Write `reports/methodology-comparison.md`:
1. **Overview table** — one row per paper: design, data/sample (N), setup, metrics, baselines, statistical testing, reproducibility (data/code available).
2. **Approach families** — group papers by method; for each group: typical strengths, weaknesses, and which papers [@key].
3. **Comparable results** — compare numbers only between papers sharing dataset, metric and setup; say explicitly when results are not comparable and why.

LAB={"V":"VERIFIED","A":"AUTHOR-CLAIM","I":"INTERPRETATION"}
DOWN={"strong":"moderate","moderate":"weak","weak":"weak"}
for f in sorted(glob.glob(d+"/papers/*/analysis.md")):

    fm=dict(re.findall(r"^(\w+): (.*)$",t.split("\n---",1)[0],re.M))
    design=fm.get("design","").split(";")[0].strip()[:70]
    n=fm.get("sample_size","").split(";")[0].strip()[:60]
    sec=re.search(r"## 13\..*?\n(.*?)\n## 14",t,re.S).group(1)
    pre = key=="zhou2024comparison"
    for line in sec.splitlines():
        c=[x.strip() for x in line.strip().strip("|").split("|")]
        if len(c)<5 or not re.match(r"RQ\d",c[0]): continue
        rq,claim,page,lab,st=c[0],"|".join(c[1:-3]) if len(c)>5 else c[1],c[-3],c[-2],c[-1]
        claim=claim.replace("|","/")
        ps=sorted(set(int(x) for x in re.findall(r"\d+",page)))
        src="[" + "; ".join(f"@{key}, p. {p}" for p in ps) + "]" if ps else f"[@{key}]"
        lab=LAB.get(lab.strip("[]")[:1].upper(),lab)
        note=""
        if pre: st=DOWN.get(st.lower(),st); note="preprint (strength downgraded)"
        rows.append((rq,f"| {rq} | {claim} | {src} | {lab} | {design}; N: {n} | {st} | {note} |"))

hdr="|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n"

print(len(rows),"rows")
from collections import Counter; print(Counter(r[0] for r in rows))
EOF

The critical review is finished and synthesis has started.

- **Review:** 2 reviewers checked all 20 analyses against the papers and raised 36 issues, mostly labels, attribution and arithmetic. All 36 are fixed, none were disputed, and all 20 analyses are now marked complete.
- **Evidence matrix:** 183 claims, all with page references, gathered in [evidence-matrix.md](research/2026-11-12-llm-based-vs-traditional-static-analysis/evidence-matrix.md).
- **Methodology comparison:** the academic-writer is now writing how the studies compare and where they contradict each other. After that come the gap analysis (with novelty checks) and the final report.

**Important findings from the review:**
1. **RepoAudit:** the gap between its own paper and the independent TSE study isn't a straight contradiction. The two studies used different datasets, code versions, bug types and metrics, so we'll present it as a documented tension rather than a direct clash.
2. **CASTLE:** its counts don't add up. For all 10 LLMs, true positives plus false negatives exceed the 150 vulnerable programs, so recall is calculated against inconsistent denominators.
3. **High F1 can mislead:** on balanced datasets, a tool that simply labels everything "vulnerable" gets F1 = 0.667. Several LLM results are close to that number, so we'll treat it as a field-wide weakness in the paper. It's useful material for a "methodological critique" section.

- synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5];
- function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8];

LLM performance falls with function and file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9], and evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. - same-benchmark comparisons of LLM vs SAST vs DL (only khare runs all three, with SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]);
- independent labelling and statistical testing [@li2026llm, p. 11];
- cost reporting;
- contamination control;
- true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19];
- workflow integration: none of the 58 studies reviewed by zhou2025large is integrated into developer workflows [@zhou2025large, p. 19].

A={
"RQ1":"No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11], but CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale general coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++) while most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Versus fine-tuned DL the ranking depends on dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. **Strength: weak–moderate.** Most robust pattern [I]: LLMs have higher recall, lower precision.",
"RQ2":"Evaluation setup explains much of the disagreement: label noise (39–65% correct) [@risse2025top, p. 8], exact-copy leakage up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4], balanced vs realistic class ratios that flip rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7], synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5], function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8], and custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. **Strength: moderate–strong** (consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs).",
"RQ3":"LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at < $0.20 per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18] (**moderate**). Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12], and needs a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10] (**weak/contested**). LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 per project vs minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Explainability is limited: LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11] and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9].",
"RQ4":"LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs and worst on context-dependent and crypto/policy CWEs and on localising memory-safety bugs [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]; CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. LLM performance falls with function/file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9]; evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. **Strength: weak** (small per-CWE cells, divergent results).",
"RQ5":"Recurring open problems: verified, realistic, repository-level benchmarks with context [@zhou2025large, p. 19; @sheng2025llms, p. 25]; same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparisons (only khare runs all three, SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]); independent labelling and statistical testing [@li2026llm, p. 11]; cost reporting; contamination control; true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19]; workflow integration [@zhou2025large, p. 19]. **Strength: moderate** [I]. Candidate gaps until novelty-checked in gap-report.md.",
}
for rq,a in A.items():
    s=re.sub(rf"(## {rq}:.*?- Status: )open(\n- Current answer[^\n]*:)[^\n]*", lambda m: m.group(1)+"answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)"+m.group(2)+" "+a, s, count=1, flags=re.S)
open(p,"w").write(s)
EOF

EOF

name: find-gaps
description: Identify evidence-backed, novelty-checked research gaps and propose contributions and experiments. Use after methodology comparison, or when the user asks what is missing in the literature or what they could research.
---

# Find research gaps

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) §7 (gap and novelty rules) is binding.

Delegate to the `gap-analyst` agent with the project id (it follows these steps); review its report before showing the user.

## 1. Collect candidate gaps
Sources, all in the project: future-work sections (analysis §11), recurring limitations (§8–9), validity threats (§10), contradictions in `evidence-matrix.md`, field-wide weaknesses in `reports/methodology-comparison.md`, RQs with weak or no answer in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`. Classify each: evidence, methodological, population/context, theoretical, practical, contradiction.

## 2. Evidence test
Keep a candidate only if at least one analysed paper supports it with `[@key, p. N]`; a gap stated by ≥2 independent papers is stronger.

## 3. Novelty check (per surviving candidate)
- ≥3 targeted `rlab search` queries across ≥2 sources, including the last 2 years (`--from`).
- One WebSearch for very recent preprints/work.
- Read titles/abstracts of the closest hits. If a hit fills the gap, drop or narrow the gap. If it is highly relevant, recommend adding it to the project.
Record date, queries and closest hits in the gap entry.

## 4. Contributions and experiments
For each gap: potential contribution, a concrete study design (data, sample, method, baseline, metrics, analysis, expected validity threats), and beginner feasibility (easy/moderate/hard and why).

## 5. Write and check
Fill `gap-report.md` using its template, ranked by evidence strength × feasibility. `rlab cite-check <id> research/<id>/gap-report.md` passes.

Done when: every listed gap has evidence, a recorded novelty check and a confidence rating. Tick Gaps in `STATUS.md`. Tell the user the top 3 gaps in plain language.

---
name: research-report
description: Generate a plain-language research report summarising a project's findings, evidence strength, gaps and next steps for a beginner researcher. Use at the end of a research run, or when the user asks for a summary, report or "what did we find".
---

# Research report

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md). The `academic-writer` agent may draft it; you check it.

Write `reports/research-report-YYYY-MM-DD.md` (new file each time; earlier reports stay):

1. **Summary in plain language** — 5–8 sentences a newcomer understands.
2. **What we did** — sources, searches, papers found/included, full-text vs abstract-only counts (from `rlab status <id>`).
3. **Answers to the research questions** — per RQ: answer, evidence strength (strong/moderate/weak), key sources `[@key, p. N]`, and what would change the answer.
4. **Key papers to read first** — 3–5 papers with one line each on why.
5. **Where studies disagree** — contradictions and likely reasons.
6. **Research gaps and possible contributions** — top gaps from `gap-report.md` with confidence, suggested study and beginner feasibility.
7. **Limitations of this review** — coverage, missing full texts, preprints, search date.
8. **Recommended next steps** — concrete actions for the user (papers to obtain, decisions to make, a first experiment).
9. **Glossary** — research terms used, one plain sentence each.

Check: `rlab cite-check <id> <report file>` passes. Update `STATUS.md` Next actions and `rlab log <id> writing "report generated: <file>"`.

Done when: all 9 sections exist, cite-check passes, and the user received a ≤10-line summary with the file path.

content.text:
The gap analysis is done, and the final research report is now being written.

**How novel our paper is (medium confidence):** I found no review that combines both of these:
- a head-to-head comparison of LLMs, SAST and deep learning together;
- an explanation of why the studies contradict each other, traced to their evaluation setup.

That combination is your paper's distinct contribution. There is one competing 2026 review (in the journal Computers and Artificial Intelligence) that makes a similar point about benchmark problems, but it doesn't cover SAST. We'll have to cite it in the paper.

**Top 3 gaps:**
1. **G1 (easy, medium–high confidence):** nobody has re-scored published results against a "flag everything" baseline or against realistic vulnerability rates. We can do this from the published numbers alone, with no experiments, and put it in your review as a table. That will make the paper stronger.
2. **G2 (moderate, medium confidence):** no study compares LLMs, SAST and deep learning on the same real, cleaned code written after the models' training cutoff. This is a good candidate for a future experimental paper.
3. **G3 (easy–moderate, low–medium confidence):** when LLMs filter SAST alarms, nobody has measured per vulnerability type how many real vulnerabilities get thrown away.

**Decision for you (no rush):** the gap analysis recommends adding about 4 more papers. The competing review is one of them and must be cited. That would take us past the 20-paper target. Once the report is finished I'll ask you whether to add them.

  ## qin2026review · ready · full-text · relevance high
  **Summary:** A single-author narrative review with 32 references (2019–2026). It sorts methods into lightweight code Transformers versus large LLMs, and its central argument is that benchmark gains are inflated by duplicates, label noise, random splits and temporal leakage. It recommends a workflow where SAST tools generate candidates, an LLM ranks and explains them, and a human confirms.
  
  **The points you asked about:**
  - **Protocol and corpus:** No search protocol, databases, screening, PRISMA, quality assessment or stated time window. The only inclusion rule is "directly analyze source code" (p. 4). The corpus is the 32-entry reference list, several of which are themselves surveys.
  - **SAST coverage:** Explicitly out of scope ("does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods", p. 4). It still concludes that LLMs and SAST complement each other (p. 12), but cites only two references for this ([1] and Gnieciak [15]) and gives no numbers.
  - **Hybrids:** Covered only conceptually (pp. 8, 13). The evidence cited is GRACE, DLAP and one context-enhancement study. None of the SAST+LLM detection or alarm-filtering studies we have are included (IRIS, RepoAudit, du2026reducing, xiong2026sifting, li2026llm).
  - **Contradictions explained by evaluation setup:** Only in general terms. Table 2 is a risk matrix (pp. 10–11), and there is one worked example, a re-reading of PrimeVul Table V (p. 12). There is no study-by-study mapping of conflicting results to their setups. Its PrimeVul numbers match our ding2025vulnerability analysis.
  - **Venue concerns:** Zeus Press journal (p. 1). The PDF has no received/accepted dates and no peer-review statement. OpenAlex lists no host organisation and shows it as not in DOAJ and not core; publication date 2026-10-29, cited_by 0. The text is inconsistent: three research questions in the introduction, four in §3.1, and an undefined "C2" (p. 12). I advise weighting it like grey literature and citing it for positioning only. I did not confirm that the venue is predatory.
  
  **Evidence rows:**
  | RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | RQ2 | Gains inflated by duplicates, label noise, random/temporal splits, model-version changes; random-split F1 = "within-benchmark performance" | 1, 10 | A | weak |
  | RQ2 | PrimeVul Table V re-read: F1 62.88–68.26% (BigVul) vs 1.91–5.82% (BigVul→PrimeVul) vs 18.05–21.43% (PrimeVul→PrimeVul) | 12 | A | moderate |
  | RQ2 | GRACE/DLAP/context enhancement/M2CVD cannot be ranked because datasets, models and protocols differ | 12 | A | weak |
  | RQ1 | SAST more stable within its rules, LLMs better at explanation; complementarity, not replacement (no numbers) | 12 | A | weak |
  | RQ3 | SAST candidates → LLM ranking/explanation → human confirmation; judge by audit time and false negatives, not F1 | 8, 13 | A | weak |
  | RQ3 | Cost items listed (API, GPU memory, latency, version drift, prompt maintenance); none quantified | 9, 12 | A | weak |
  | RQ5 | Out-of-time + project-isolated tests, data cards, calibration, recall at a fixed false-positive budget, explanation verification, audit-time studies | 13 | A | weak |
  
  ## lu2025lab · ready · full-text · relevance high
  **Summary:** Four DL detectors were trained on Juliet, Devign, BigVul and ICVul, then ReVeal and LineVul were tested on VentiVul, a new set of Linux and Chromium CVEs disclosed from 2025-05-01 (200 CVEs, 263 vulnerable/patched function pairs, about 2% vulnerable). Four open-weight LLMs were tested on the same data without fine-tuning. In-distribution DL F1 of 91–94.5 collapses to 3.47–8.65, and the LLMs reach 0.79–5.36 conservative F1, with patch-pair accuracy under 6% for every model.
  
  **Venue status:** arXiv v4 (4 Nov 2026), whose footnote says "accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software" (p. 1). There is no JSS DOI in metadata, so I flagged it as "not peer-reviewed (author-reported JSS acceptance)".
  
  **DL vs LLM, in-distribution vs temporally separated:**
  - **DL in-distribution:**
    - LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul 91.00 on BigVul (pp. 11–12).
    - On BigVul, ReVeal/Devign/VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45/94.09/94.39 but F1 only 23.58/16.90/0.19 (p. 11).
  - **DL cross-dataset:** LineVul trained on BigVul scores 0 / 1.90 / 13.05 on the other three datasets (p. 12).
  - **DL on VentiVul:**
    - F1 3.47–8.65; best is ReVeal trained on BigVul at 8.65 (precision 5.25, recall 24.43). LineVul trained on BigVul gets 6.87 (p. 13).
    - Patch-pair accuracy (PACC) is under 5.5% for all DL models; best 5.34 (p. 13).
  - **LLMs:** only evaluated on VentiVul, so there are no in-distribution LLM numbers. LLM precision and recall are not reported.
    - Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3-30B 3.09, Mistral-24B 4.07.
    - Best overall is Mistral few-shot: F1 5.36, CVE detection rate 46%, PACC 5.75.
    - Highest valid-only F1 is Qwen2.5 with chain-of-thought at 8.21 (3.04 conservative) (p. 14).
  
  **Evidence rows:**
  | RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | RQ2 | DL in-distribution F1 high (94.52/94.14 Juliet, 91.00 BigVul) but drops cross-dataset (LineVul-BigVul → 0/1.90/13.05) | 11, 12 | V | moderate |
  | RQ2 | Accuracy hides failure at 6% prevalence: BigVul accuracy 87–94 with F1 23.58/16.90/0.19 | 11 | V | moderate |
  | RQ1 | On VentiVul (~2% prevalence), trained DL F1 3.47–8.65 | 13 | V | moderate |
  | RQ1 | 4 open-weight LLMs on the same functions: conservative F1 0.79–5.36, PACC < 6%; zero-shot CVE detection rate 5–34%, below most DL configs | 13, 14 | V | moderate |
  | RQ1 | Both families are near an all-positive baseline (F1 ≈ 3.9%) | 4, 13 | I | moderate |
  | RQ2 | CVE detection rate 94.59–100% with PACC 0–0.76% for Devign/ICVul-trained models; all DL PACC < 5.5% | 13 | V | moderate |
  | RQ4 | Project/CWE variance: LineVul-BigVul CVE detection 76% Chromium vs 0% Linux; best per-CWE PACC 18.18% on small cells | 13, 14 | V | weak |
  | RQ2 | Prompting effects depend on model and metric (few-shot helps only Mistral; chain-of-thought lowers Qwen2.5 PACC) | 13 | V | weak |
  | RQ5 | Separation by release date cannot rule out LLM contamination; "unrelated" functions may carry residual label noise | 17 | A | moderate |
  
  ## Surprising or doubtful
  - **Results near chance:** The paper never compares its scores with a chance baseline. By my calculation (263/13,326 ≈ 2% vulnerable), an all-positive predictor scores F1 ≈ 3.9%. LineVul trained on Devign (recall 100, precision 2, F1 3.93) is effectively that predictor, and most LLM conservative F1 values fall at or below it.
  - **Uneven DL vs LLM comparison:** The LLMs are mid-size open-weight models (two are mixture-of-experts with 2.4–3B active parameters), not fine-tuned, with Qwen3 thinking mode off. Inputs are single functions with no context. There are no SAST tools, no frontier LLMs and no cost figures.
  - **Wrong reason recorded for adding lu2025lab:** The `added_reason` in its `metadata.json` cites "WordPress PHP" label quality and "G6 cost/energy". The paper is C/C++ only and reports no cost or energy, so that reason seems to belong to a different paper. I did not edit the metadata; the gap report should not use lu2025lab for G6 or the PHP point.
  - **Qin as a competitor:** Its weak venue and lack of a protocol make it a manageable competitor. Our differences from it are a systematic method, SAST treated as a reviewed family, empirical hybrid evidence, and contradictions mapped study by study to evaluation setup. It still needs to be cited.
  
  ## Sections not completed
  None. The figures were images: Qin's Figures 1–2 I read from the PDF page images. For lu2025lab's Figures 3–7, numbers come from the results text, not from reading the bar charts.

The 2 new papers' analyses are done.

- **The competing review (Qin, CAI 2026):** it turned out to be a weak competitor. - **"From Lab to Reality":** on vulnerabilities disclosed after May 2025, deep learning models got F1 3–9% and LLMs 1–5%. A tool that flags everything would get about 3.9% on this data, so both are close to chance. This is strong support for G1 and G2.

One small note: when I added 3 papers in one batch I gave them a single shared reason, so lu2025lab's recorded "reason" also mentions PHP and cost. The correct per-paper reasons are in screening.md.

**Waiting on you:** download the 2 MDPI PDFs (links in my previous message), then tell me "downloaded".

# graphify
- **graphify** (`~/.claude/skills/graphify/SKILL.md`) - any input to knowledge graph. Trigger: `/graphify`
When the user types `/graphify`, use the installed graphify skill or instructions before doing anything else.

# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, reading-guide, resume-research.

name: compare-methods
description: Compare methodologies, datasets, metrics and findings across a project's analysed papers, consolidate the evidence matrix and identify contradictions. Use after paper analyses are complete, or when the user asks how studies differ or agree.
---

# Compare methodologies

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) §1, §5, §6.

Input: project id. Use only analyses with `status: ready` or `complete`; `rlab index <id>` then read `literature-matrix.md` for the overview, and each `papers/*/analysis.md` for detail.

## 1. Evidence matrix
Merge every analysis's evidence table (section 13) into `evidence-matrix.md`, one row per claim, Source as `[@key, p. N]`. Keep the paper's label; downgrade strength for abstract-only and preprint sources.

## 2. Methodology comparison
Write `reports/methodology-comparison.md`:
1. **Overview table** — one row per paper: design, data/sample (N), setup, metrics, baselines, statistical testing, reproducibility (data/code available).
2. **Approach families** — group papers by method; for each group: typical strengths, weaknesses, and which papers [@key].
3. **Comparable results** — compare numbers only between papers sharing dataset, metric and setup; say explicitly when results are not comparable and why.
4. **Contradictions** — copy to `evidence-matrix.md` "Contradictions": claims, sources, differences in data/population/method/metric/time, possible explanation labelled [I].
5. **Methodological weaknesses across the field** — recurring problems (small N, no baselines, no significance tests, leakage risk, no code). These feed gap finding.
6. **What this means for our RQs** — per RQ, current answer with evidence strength; update "Current answer" in `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.

## 3. Check
`rlab cite-check <id> research/<id>/evidence-matrix.md research/<id>/reports/methodology-comparison.md` passes.

Done when: every ready/complete paper appears in the overview table, every RQ has a current answer with strength, cite-check passes. Tick Synthesis in `STATUS.md`.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/makky/Downloads/AI-Research-Lab-main/.claude/skills/start-research

# Start research

Run from the workspace root. `rlab` means `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md). You are the orchestrator: follow [.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md](../../agents/research-orchestrator.md) for delegation and state ownership.

After every phase: tick it in `STATUS.md`, rewrite "Next actions", `rlab log <id> <phase> "<what happened>"`, and give the user a 1–3 line progress update in plain language.

## 1. Scope
Judge whether the topic is researchable as stated. It is **too broad or ambiguous** when it spans several fields, has no clear population/context/outcome, or would plausibly return hundreds of relevant papers.
- Too broad/ambiguous: ask up to 3 multiple-choice questions (AskUserQuestion), each option explained in one plain sentence, with your recommended option first.
- Otherwise: choose sensible defaults (last ~10 years, peer-reviewed first, ≤20 included papers) and record them as assumptions.

Done when: scope, time window and target size are fixed.

## 2. Create the project
`rlab new "<topic>"` → note the project id it prints.

## 3. Objectives and research questions
1. Pilot search to learn the field's vocabulary: `rlab search <id> "<topic keywords>" --limit 10`.
2. Fill `RESEARCH.md`: plain-language topic, scope, 2–4 objectives, inclusion/exclusion criteria, 3–6 facet queries in the search strategy, assumptions under "Key decisions".
3. Fill `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`: 3–5 questions, each answerable from literature, linked to an objective.
4. Show the user the objectives and questions (≤10 lines) and invite corrections. Continue unless they object.

Done when: both files have no empty required fields and Scoping is ticked.

## 4. Discover and screen
Follow the `discover-papers` skill.

## 5. Acquire full texts
`rlab fetch <id>`. For each `NONE` result, list the paper in STATUS "Blocked / needs user" and tell the user once, in one message: which papers lack open access, and that they can download them via their library and run `rlab attach <id> <key> <file.pdf>` (or give you the files). Continue: those papers are analysed abstract-only until a PDF arrives.

Done when: every paper has fulltext status `downloaded`, `user-supplied` or `unavailable`.

## 6. Analyse
Follow the `analyze-paper` skill for every paper, delegated to `paper-analyst` agents in parallel (3–4 papers per agent).

Done when: every paper's analysis is `ready`.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
</system-reminder>

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

The user may see only the question dialog: tool results and text you wrote earlier in this turn may not be on their screen while it is open. Make each question stand on its own: if it depends on something you found, say so briefly, and name the items you are asking about in the question itself.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- `cd` carries to the next call only in the main session, if the command succeeds and ends inside the working directories. Outside them the shell returns to the start folder; otherwise it stays where it was. Prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
